Latest Update: Hyundai claims 2027’s ‘Best EV Brand’ title as the IONIQ 5 and IONIQ 9 impress

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (723 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Hyundai’s electric SUVs are getting some love.
  • “This win showcases the breadth and strength of Hyundai’s SUV and electric lineups,” Alex Kwanten, managing editor at Autos at US News, remarked after naming it the Best EV Brand and Best SUV Brand for 2027.
  • This marks the first time Hyundai has earned the Best EV Brand award and the third consecutive win for Best SUV Brand.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Hyundai’s electric SUVs are getting some love. The IONIQ 5 and three-row IONIQ 9 helped the Korean automaker land its first-ever “Best Electric Vehicle Brand” award from US News & World Report for 2027.

“This win showcases the breadth and strength of Hyundai’s SUV and electric lineups,” Alex Kwanten, managing editor at Autos at US News, remarked after naming it the Best EV Brand and Best SUV Brand for 2027.

This marks the first time Hyundai has earned the Best EV Brand award and the third consecutive win for Best SUV Brand.

Including hybrid and electric vehicles, Hyundai offers ten unique SUVs, “many of them at or near the top of our rankings in those classes for capability, comfort, performance and value,” Kwanten mentioned.

Hyundai’s fully electric SUVs, the IONIQ 5 and IONIQ 9, “in particular, stand out for their combination of style and technology,” he explained.

Hyundai presently offers the IONIQ 5, including the sporty IONIQ 5 N and off-road-focused IONIQ 5 XRT, plus the three-row IONIQ 9.

Although Hyundai discontinued its electric sedan, the IONIQ 6, after the 2025 model year, the new high-performance IONIQ 6 N joins the lineup in 2027.

The IONIQ 5 continued to earn praise, taking its third consecutive Best Compact Electric SUV award. Its larger sibling, the IONIQ 9, took the top spot in the midsize electric SUV category.

Hyundai’s IONIQ 5 is the most popular EV in the US this year through September that isn’t a Tesla, ranking third behind the Model Y and Model 3.

Industry observers note that why does it continue winning over buyers? The IONIQ 5 checks all the boxes with long-range capabilities, fast charging, and a surprisingly spacious interior with modern tech.

It’s also among the most affordable EVs in the US. Prices for the 2027 Hyundai IONIQ 5 start at just $35,250.

Industry observers note that however, the base price is for the standard-range IONIQ 5 SE with an EPA-estimated range of up to 245 miles. Upgrading to the extended-range SE RWD model costs an extra $2,500, with prices starting at $37,750, but it offers up to 318 miles of range.

The three-row Hyundai IONIQ 9 electric SUV starts at $58,955 with an EPA-estimated range of up to 335 miles.

According to recent reports, hyundai’s IONIQ 5 is about the size of a Tesla Model Y, with two rows of seating and space for five passengers. Hyundai’s larger IONIQ 9 offers three rows of seating with six- or seven-seat options.

The larger IONIQ 9 offers up to 163.54 cubic feet of interior passenger volume, compared with up to 106.5 cubic feet in the IONIQ 5.

Both electric SUVs use an 800-volt electrical architecture for ultra-fast charging. The IONIQ 5 can charge from 10% to 80% in about 20 minutes, while the IONIQ 9 takes around 24 minutes using a 350 kW DC fast charger.

Hyundai assembles the IONIQ 5 and IONIQ 9 at the Hyundai Motor Group Metaplant America outside of Savannah, Georgia.

When we toured the facility earlier this year, Hyundai told Electrek that its electric SUVs are winning over new buyers at a higher rate than any of its gas or hybrid vehicles.

The IONIQ 5 had a 69.8% conquest rate last year, while the IONIQ 9 had 64.3%. Hyundai’s Elantra N ranked third (61.9%), followed by the Palisade (61.2%) and Kona Electric (60.9%).

In a recent development, is Hyundai the best Electric Vehicle brand in your opinion? While Hyundai took the top spot overall, Lucid remained the Best Luxury EV Brand for the second consecutive year. Hyundai’s Genesis also repeated as Best Luxury Brand. Share your thoughts in the comments below.

Potatoes grown in moon dirt are as nutritious as Earth potatoes

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (577 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Astronauts living in the first permanent lunar base may see a sizable number of spuds on their dinner plates.
  • Industry observers note that “We found that potatoes can complete their entire life cycle in simulated lunar soil when supplemented with organic matter,” Aymeric Goyer, an OSU botanist and study co-author, said in a statement.
  • It has been revealed that even in a controlled habitat, life on the moon will be physically demanding for astronauts.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Astronauts living in the first permanent lunar base may see a sizable number of spuds on their dinner plates. In a study published today in the journal npj Microgravity, botanists at Oregon State University (OSU) proved it’s possible to grow healthy, edible potatoes in simulated moon soil with the help of everyday worms. Importantly, the team also identified the proper proportions of lunar regolith and compost needed to produce potato yields similar to those grown on Earth.

Industry observers note that “We found that potatoes can complete their entire life cycle in simulated lunar soil when supplemented with organic matter,” Aymeric Goyer, an OSU botanist and study co-author, said in a statement. “That’s an important step toward developing reliable food production systems that could support long-term human exploration of the Moon.”.

It has been revealed that even in a controlled habitat, life on the moon will be physically demanding for astronauts. They’ll require carefully maintained, nutritious diets to keep them healthy, but it’s not as simple as sending them off packed with calorically dense prepackaged meals. Cargo room on spacecraft is limited and costly, and the desolate lunar surface isn’t exactly hospitable to agriculture. In addition to constant bombardment by cosmic and solar radiation, temperatures can swing anywhere between 250 degrees and -410 degrees Fahrenheit.

Recent findings suggest that indoor horticulture will also be challenging. Lunar regolith is an annoyingly powdery substance composed of sharp-edged, miniscule particles created over billions of years of asteroid impacts, but little else. With essentially no organic material at all, the dust alone isn’t capable of supporting plant life.

In a recent development, while it is easy enough to combine that lunar regolith with agricultural additives, researchers weren’t sure if these could overcome moon soil’s heavy metals and irradiation. To test it, Goyer and his colleagues first obtained simulated lunar regolith made to resemble the samples collected during the Apollo missions. Regolith composition varies by region on the moon, so they selected five different types based on darker lunar mare dust and the lighter lunar highland soil. They then mixed the mock moon dust with vermicompost, the nutrient-rich soil created when worms break down organic materials. Next, they planted potatoes in various ratios of regolith and vermicompost, and monitored their growth. As a control, the team even planted potatoes in soil taken from Hermiston, Oregon, an area famous for some of the world’s highest spud yields.

The team found that composite soil with only 30 percent vermicompost was enough to produce potato crops comparable to those farmed on Earth. Their findings suggest the supplemental organics bind to the regolith’s heavy metals, which shield the plants and minimize any damage to their roots.

“We believe the compost helps balance some of the toxicity we see in lunar regolith,” added OSU botanist and study co-author David Handy.

Sources indicate that but bushels of moon potatoes only go so far if they lack any real nutritional value. Even here, the lunar simulations offered promising results, particularly when it came to glycoalkaloids. The naturally forming potato toxins can cause green skin discoloration, but analysis indicated no statistically relevant rise in glycoalkaloids for the lunar crops.

With the potato viability debate settled, Goyer’s team will next compare 10 specific spud varieties grown in simulated lunar regolith to determine the most nutritious and resilient options for NASA astronomers.

6 to 8 Cups of Tea Daily May Reduce Heart Disease Risk by 11%

📅 28 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (618 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Healthline

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • People who regularly drink tea may have an 11% lower overall risk of vascular disease, which includes conditions such as stroke, heart disease, and peripheral artery disease.
  • Both black tea and green tea may offer heart health benefits.
  • The lowest overall vascular risk was seen among tea drinkers who were also physically active and didn’t smoke.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

People who regularly drink tea may have an 11% lower overall risk of vascular disease, which includes conditions such as stroke, heart disease, and peripheral artery disease. This is according to a study published on October 21 in the Journal of Internal Medicine.

Both black tea and green tea may offer heart health benefits. However, the study shows an association rather than proving that drinking tea prevents cardiovascular disease.

The lowest overall vascular risk was seen among tea drinkers who were also physically active and didn’t smoke.

The study followed 485,934 people ages 30–79 from the China Kadoorie Biobank for an average of 9 years.

The researchers found that regular tea drinkers had an 11% lower overall risk of vascular disease compared with those who did not regularly drink tea. They also observed a 37% lower risk of ischemic stroke and a 17% lower risk of heart attack.

There was no clear link for hemorrhagic stroke or pulmonary heart disease.

Among people who drank tea at least weekly, the lowest estimated risk was seen in those consuming approximately 6–8 cups per day. However, the findings do not establish this as a recommended daily intake.

Amit Blumfield, MD, a cardiologist with Manhattan Cardiology in NYC who wasn’t involved in the study, told Healthline that it is crucial to remember this is observational data.

Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) examining the effects of drinking black and green tea on lipids and blood pressure highlighted only modest, non-significant benefits.

The study also had limitations, including self-reported tea consumption and the possibility that other dietary and lifestyle factors influenced the results.

“Overall, tea seems to, maybe, have some cardiovascular benefits without a significant risk, so I favor tea consumption,” he said.

Michelle Routhenstein, a preventive cardiology dietitian at Entirely Nourished who was not involved in the research, emphasized that the findings do not establish a cause-and-effect relationship between drinking tea and a lower risk of vascular disease.

“Tea can be a helpful addition to a heart-healthy lifestyle, but it is not a substitute for addressing individual cardiovascular risk factors,” she mentioned.

The researchers also found that drinking “burning hot” tea increased the risk of vascular disease by 16%, consistent with previous research raising concerns about the consumption of very hot beverages.

“I recommend enjoying your tea’s potential benefits by letting it cool to a comfortable sipping temperature before you drink it,” said Routhenstein.

The study examined black, green, Oolong, and other tea types.

Industry observers note that the researchers found that black tea highlighted a more consistent association with a lower risk of vascular disease, which is contrary to some earlier research. However, they noted that these results don’t establish black tea as superior to green tea, and they don’t mean you should switch tea types.

“Both black and green tea are great choices for your heart health, and neither is definitively better than the other,” remarked Routhenstein.

“I recommend choosing whichever you enjoy and consuming it consistently, ideally without much added sugar,” Routhenstein noted.

Blumfield also noted that adding sugar or non-sugar sweeteners may change the potential health effects of drinking tea, so the findings should not automatically be extended to sweetened tea beverages.

Sources indicate that some older research suggests there may be additional health benefits to drinking both black and green tea. These benefits may include:.

Routhenstein remarked that tea may also support focus and alertness, improve hydration status, and potentially play a role in metabolic health.

“Enjoying tea can be a simple way to incorporate beneficial plant compounds into your day,” she added.

While drinking tea has been considered a health-promoting habit since ancient times, more research is needed to confirm its various health benefits.

In a recent development, kia’s EV lineup covers just about every size and price point, but it believes one thing is still missing: a truly cheap electric car. That’s about to change in 2027, when Kia looks to unveil a new EV that could start at around $22,000 to $24,000.

It’s been 40 years since Kia introduced its first electric vehicle, the Besta EV, created so runners in the 1986 Asian Games wouldn’t have to breathe toxic fumes from the broadcast vehicle.

Kia has come a long way since the Besta EV hit the road, now offering a complete lineup of electric vehicles, from compact SUVs and hatchbacks to vans and three-row SUVs.

In Europe and the UK, Kia’s electric lineup consists of the EV2, EV3, EV4, EV5, EV6, EV9, and PV5 van, but the Korean automaker isn’t done yet.

“With no intention of resting on its laurels,” Kia remarked, the brand intends to complete development of its first software-defined vehicle (SDV) by the end of 2027, an all-fresh B-segment EV hatchback.

It didn’t offer any other details on the upcoming EV, but Ted Lee, Kia’s executive vice president and head of global operations, told Auto Express that Kia and Hyundai are co-developing a new dedicated EV architecture for an upcoming pair of entry-level electric cars.

Expected to arrive as the Hyundai IONIQ 1 and Kia EV1, the upcoming EVs will compete with other entry-level electric cars like the Renault Twingo, which starts at about €20,000.

It has been revealed that lee remarked the EV1’s price will be highly competitive not just with other entry-level EVs, but also with small gas-powered cars, with prices expected to start in the €20,000 to €22,000 range, or about $22,000 to $24,000. And that’s without government incentives.

The EV2 starts at just €26,600 ($29,500) in Germany and other European markets as Kia’s current entry-level EV, so the price range would make sense.

While it will be Kia’s cheapest EV, Lee promised it would not cut corners in quality, design, or features.

As its first SDV, the EV1 will feature Kia and Hyundai Motor’s latest-generation tech and software. Kia stated the electric SDV will offer Level 2+ autonomous driving on highways. In 2029, Kia plans to expand to Level 2++, enabling it to operate in cities.

The new EV will also use Hyundai’s SDV architecture (CODA), the Pleos Connect infotainment system, and Gleo AI, an in-vehicle Agenic AI.

Industry observers note that what will the EV1 look like? According to Auto Express, the entry-level EV will look a bit sportier and less boxy than the EV2 SUV. It could draw inspiration from the Vision Meta Turismo concept.

It also apparently won’t be based on the Picanto, Kia’s smallest gas-powered car. The Kia EV1 is expected to bring a unique style to the family.

This is good to see and makes sense, especially in Europe. I don't think Kia can go wrong making vehicles at so many different price points. It allows them to reach different segments and almost literally have something for almost everyone.

While all of Kia’s current EVs feature its ccNC infotainment system with dual 12.3″ instrument display and infotainment screens, plus a 5″ climate control panel, the EV1 could bring a simpler setup.

Sources indicate that like its other electric models, the EV1 is expected to receive the GT treatment. However, as an entry-level model, it may not use a dual-motor all-wheel-drive setup like the others.

Will Kia bring the EV1 to the US? Don’t get your hopes up. Kia has previously mentioned the B-segment hatchback is designed for Europe. It could even be built alongside the EV2 at Kia’s plant in Slovakia.

The good news? The EV3, Kia’s compact electric SUV, is now on sale in the US, starting at just $29,890.

The hotel staff immediately recognized the dog, but not because of her sparkling personality or floppy ears. Becky’s owner has dementia, and the unnamed man has disappeared before.

According to recent reports, the team at Whiteface called the Fresh York State Police (NYSP), who contacted the Department of Conservation (DEC) Forest Rangers for assistance with the search. Four NYSP officers and 14 Rangers used drones and another dog (a bloodhound) to search for the missing person. According to Charlie Foutch, the lead Ranger on the search, it was about 25 to 30 degrees Fahrenheit overnight.

Recent findings suggest that at 10 a.m. the next morning, a hunter who was searching just ahead of the group heard someone fall and scream. He found the missing man off to the side of a trail in a draining area with open woods. Ranger Sabo arrived on the scene shortly after. The 69-year-old man was not wearing gloves or shoes, and was suffering from some frostbite on his feet and hands. He was still alert and talking.

Recent findings suggest that “We’re always looking for live people. That’s our goal is to find a live person,” said Fouch. “And a lot of people are really tough. This gentleman didn’t have shoes on when we found him in the morning or mittens or gloves, so he had been out there for some period of time at night. And he still did okay. Sometimes if you keep moving in that situation, you generate enough heat to do okay.”.

It has been revealed that due to his injuries and the location off the trail, a hoist was the safest and quickest way to get him to safety. Ranger Martin used a cable to hoist him up to a helicopter, while NYSP Pilot Engle flew them to the hospital.

In addition to this coordination between hunters, the NYSP, and DEC, Fouch noted that Becky the basset hound made this happy ending possible.

“I think if the dog had not shown up at Whiteface, that gentleman definitely would have had a different outcome,” said Fouch. “It definitely would have been much harder to find him. He may not have survived the rest of the day and probably not another night. The dog definitely contributed to him being saved so quickly.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • New data show a substantial nationwide increase in potentially deadly infections caused by drug-resistant pathogens.
  • The updated Antimicrobial Resistance (AR) Threats Report from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) states that drug-resistant bacteria and fungi cause approximately 9.7 million infections in the United States each year.
  • The estimated deaths in the United States from these drug-resistant pathogens have also risen from 35,000 to 50,800.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

New data show a substantial nationwide increase in potentially deadly infections caused by drug-resistant pathogens.

The updated Antimicrobial Resistance (AR) Threats Report from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) states that drug-resistant bacteria and fungi cause approximately 9.7 million infections in the United States each year. This is up from 2.8 million in a similar report from 2019.

The estimated deaths in the United States from these drug-resistant pathogens have also risen from 35,000 to 50,800.

The new report also noted that infections that commonly occur in people in the hospital account for more than 42,000 deaths and cost the U.S. healthcare system more than $12 billion.

It has been revealed that these findings are based on 2023 data. Officials from the CDC stated that the increase in drug-resistant infections from 2019 partially reflects a real rise in infections caused by certain resistant bacteria and fungi. However, they also noted that data sources and methodologies have changed, and direct comparisons between the two reports shouldn’t be made.

“These numbers are alarming by any measure but are particularly sobering when infectious diseases physicians connect real patients with these statistics in their everyday experience,” Wendy Armstrong, MD, President of the Infectious Diseases Society of America (IDSA), noted in a statement.

The CDC report highlighted 19 drug-resistant pathogens responsible for the 9.7 million annual infections. Four of these pathogens are classified as urgent threats, 13 as serious threats, and 2 as concerning.

The CDC also maintains a watch list that currently includes six pathogens.

The four pathogens classified as urgent threats are:.

William Schaffner, MD, a professor of the Division of Infectious Diseases at Vanderbilt University Medical Center, told Healthline that the reason for this increase in superbugs is, “Overuse of antibiotics; using them for too long or in circumstances where they do not offer a benefit.”.

According to recent reports, “An example of the latter is the antibiotic treatment of common viral respiratory infections — antibiotics have no effect on viral infections. The widespread use of antibiotics kills off those bacteria that are susceptible to antibiotics, but then can leave a few bacterial survivors that are resistant to the effect of the antibiotics, resulting in the spread of these resistant strains,” he noted.

Monica Gandhi, MD, a professor of medicine at the University of California, San Francisco, agreed and added, “This widespread use leads to selective drug pressure on the pathogen to evolve resistance to these antibiotics, making them harder to treat.”.

It has been revealed that “The risk to public health from these bugs is substantial. In fact, the World Health Organization (WHO) estimates up to 5 million deaths from these bugs worldwide every year, making these a substantial public health threat,” said Gandhi.

Candida auris tops the list of urgent threats.

According to recent reports, cases have increased nearly tenfold since the first detection in hospitals 10 years ago. This includes a more than 50% jump between 2022 and 2023.

Sources indicate that candida auris is a fungus that is almost completely resistant to one class of antifungal medications. It has also shown emerging resistance to the other two classes.

This fungus is often found on people’s skin, spreads rapidly in healthcare settings like hospitals, and affects some of the most vulnerable individuals.

CRE is a family of multidrug-resistant bacterial pathogens. They have become increasingly difficult to treat and can share resistance with other bacteria.

Sources indicate that these bacteria also pose a significant threat to people in hospitals, especially those with devices such as ventilators and catheters. A recent study found that CRE cases at U.S. hospitals increased by 18% between 2019 and 2023.

While those in hospitals are especially vulnerable to CRE, 67% of the cases in 2023 were in the community. However, some of these cases may have occurred in people with recent exposure to healthcare.

Neisseria gonorrhoeae is the bacterium that causes gonorrhea, which is one of the most common sexually transmitted infections.

The CDC report noted that only a few antibiotics can effectively treat this infection.

Without effective treatment, gonorrhea can lead to:.

There are ways you can help prevent these superbugs:.

“[One] way individuals can help prevent the evolution of these superbugs is to not ask for antibiotics from their providers or urgent care settings in the setting of a viral infection,” said Gandhi.

Experts and organizations like the CDC are working together to find ways to reduce the spread of these superbugs.

“Professional organizations and hospitals are educating their doctors and staff about the antibiotic resistance problem and have created reviews of practice patterns to encourage the appropriate use of antibiotics,” said Schaffner.

Gandhi added that organizations should institute procedures, such as “antimicrobial stewardship programs,” to ensure that providers do not prescribe antibiotics for non-bacterial infections and narrow antibiotics as soon as possible.

The Pioneering Antimicrobial Subscriptions to End Upsurging Resistance (PASTEUR) Act aims to revitalize antibiotic and antifungal development by changing the way the federal government pays for novel antimicrobials.

This act was reintroduced in Congress in February and is currently under review.

The focus on reducing the spread of superbugs and developing new antibiotics is important.

“You really cannot have all the benefits of modern medicine, even outside the realm of infectious diseases, without effective antibiotics. It all goes away,” Haley Ann Pritchard, MD, medical director of infection prevention and antimicrobial stewardship at Eskenazi Health Hospital, stated in a statement.

#224609. Supersonic jets want a comeback. But can Americans stand the boom?

Supersonic jets want a comeback. But can Americans stand the boom?

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2457 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, in the spring of 1967, William Shurcliff began moonlighting on a project that seemed hopeless: urging the U.S.
  • So Shurcliff released the Citizens League Against the Sonic Boom and took aim at the most expensive project in U.S.
  • In 1971, Congress cut off funding for the SST, and two years later the FAA banned civilian supersonic flight over U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, in the spring of 1967, William Shurcliff began moonlighting on a project that seemed hopeless: urging the U.S. government to stop supersonic jets. By day, the Harvard-trained physicist ran experiments at the Cambridge Electron Accelerator. By night, he spent hours writing letters—to congressmen, federal aviation officials, mayors, and newspaper editors. It was not a job he wanted. “I was hoping and praying someone else would do it,” he told The Harvard Crimson.

But no one else would. So Shurcliff released the Citizens League Against the Sonic Boom and took aim at the most expensive project in U.S. commercial aviation history at the time, the Supersonic Transport (SST) program. His opposition to the SST stemmed from research by Swedish scientist Bo Lundberg, who had written extensively on the perils of supersonic aviation, chiefly the sonic boom, which could impact hundreds of millions of people every day. Shurcliff’s goal was uncompromising. “Just as the only way to get rid of the smell of the skunk is to eliminate the skunk,” he told The Upcoming York Times, “we propose to attack the sonic boom by eliminating the SST.”.

It worked. In 1971, Congress cut off funding for the SST, and two years later the FAA banned civilian supersonic flight over U.S. soil.

In a recent development, today, prompted by a 2025 executive order, the FAA is proposing to lift that ban before any community response tests of emerging supersonic technology have taken place. And even if newly introduced engineering designs can reduce the sonic booms at airliner scale, the economic and environmental costs that have plagued supersonic flight haven’t changed since Shurcliff’s day.

During World War II, Shurcliff worked at the federal Office of Scientific Research and Development, helping keep the Manhattan Project’s atomic-bomb patents secret. In 1946, he witnessed firsthand the atomic tests at Bikini Atoll and wrote the official account, Bombs at Bikini. His son later told The Newly introduced York Times that his father was so affected he spent the rest of his life atoning for that work.

In a recent development, when supersonic aviation programs began heating up in the 1960s, Shurcliff was wary of the press, but he was clear about supersonic technology. “We all believe in progress,” he told the Crimson, “but some things just aren’t progress.”.

Sources indicate that the U.S. government-sponsored SST program was the culmination of supersonic military research that began on the heels of World War II. In January 1947, months before anyone had flown faster than sound, Popular Science described Bell’s experimental XS-1, also known as the X-1, which it said might someday reach 1,700 mph, more than twice the speed of sound and three times faster than a typical commercial jet. That October, Chuck Yeager broke the sound barrier in the X-1.

In a recent development, fifteen years later, in 1962, Britain and France agreed to build Concorde, and the Soviet Union soon introduced its own supersonic airliner program, Tupolev Tu-144. The following year, President John F. Kennedy committed the U.S. to a faster, bigger rival, SST. Boeing won the contract in 1966. But even as the race heated up, an enormous problem trailed in its wake.

According to recent reports, sit in a closed room and the air feels perfectly still, but it isn’t. At room temperature, air molecules zip around at an average of about 1,000 miles per hour, each one bouncing off its neighbors billions of times a second. You don’t feel a gale because they’re flying every which way at once—for every molecule headed toward your face, another is headed away. What you’re feeling, without noticing, is the sum of all that pummeling—air pressure—about 14.7 pounds of it on every square inch (psi) of your body at sea level. You notice it only when the balance shifts, such as when the wind blows—a mass of air being pushed from high pressure toward low.

That restless jostling of air molecules is also how sound travels. A voice, a drumbeat, or a jet engine will shove the molecules, which pass along the shove like a crowd in a stadium passing along a wave even as every fan stays in place. The ricocheting molecules pass along vibrations somewhat inefficiently, which is why sound travels a bit slower than the molecules themselves, about 760 mph at sea level, and slower still in the frigid air at airplane cruising altitudes.

When a plane flies faster than the speed of sound, it outruns the air molecules carrying the wave. The air ahead gets no warning until the jet slams it aside, compressing it and creating a shock wave that trails the jet like the V-shaped wake behind a speedboat. But the shock wave’s wake is three-dimensional, spreading in a widening cone that sweeps across the ground below.

Recent findings suggest that A sonic boom isn’t a single bang that occurs the moment a plane “breaks the sound barrier.” It’s a continuous swath of jarring noise and pressure that follows the jet. Anyone in the cone’s path, or “boom carpet,” experiences it.

Sources indicate that in his 1970 explainer, S/S/T and Sonic Boom Handbook, Shurcliff estimated the boom carpet at 40 to 60 miles wide for the supersonic aircraft of his day. The jolt hits hardest directly beneath the flight path and weakens toward the cone’s edges.

Worse, Shurcliff warned, boom behavior was erratic. Swirls of wind and temperature could focus a shock wave so that one house took twice the jolt of its neighbor a few hundred feet away. That, he argued, meant people would never get used to sonic booms, just as people never get used to lightning and thunder.

On paper, booms don’t seem like they should be a big deal. A boom from supersonic passenger jets like Concorde raises air pressure at sea level about .014 psi relative to the normal 14.7 psi we live with—that’s just a 0.1 percent increase. It doesn’t seem like much, but relative to everyday sounds, it’s enormous.

Industry observers note that if you’ve ever stood near the speakers at a live concert and felt the bass or drum hit your chest, you’ve felt a pressure pulse like a sonic boom, but that bass is only 6.5 pascals, or Pa, a measure of air pressure. Now multiply that punch by about 15 and deliver it without warning. It’s roughly the shove of a 30 mph wind gust delivered in a fraction of a second and aimed at every wall and window of your house at once. That’s what the 0.1 percent of a supersonic jet actually represents.

What no one knew in the early 1960s, when supersonic research was barreling ahead, was how people would feel living under that boom carpet day after day. In 1964, the FAA decided to find out, picking Oklahoma City.

It has been revealed that in a six-month trial that began in February 1964, Oklahoma City residents were subjected to eight sonic booms a day, starting at 7 a.m., to gauge how well they would accept the disruption, and whether they would grow accustomed to it. By the end, the Oklahoma City Council had requested a halt to the flights, and the FAA had logged more than 12,000 calls, mostly complaints, alongside more than 5,000 damage claims for broken windows, cracked walls and floors, and destruction of personal property.

Despite the fallout, the following year the agency pointed to a University of Chicago survey of Oklahoma City residents as vindication. Nearly three-quarters remarked they could live with eight booms a day indefinitely. The survey’s own numbers told a different story.

In a recent development, nearly every resident surveyed, 94 percent, reported rattling walls and windows, and almost four in 10 believed the booms had damaged their homes. The longer the booms continued, the less people liked them. The share who felt more than a little annoyed rose from 37 percent to 56 percent, and those who said they could live with the booms fell from 91 percent to 73 percent during the six-month trial. Anger over the FAA’s handling of damage claims eventually turned Oklahoma Senator Mike Monroney, one of aviation’s staunchest champions, against the SST program.

Although the residents of Oklahoma City delivered mixed results, the negative data emboldened the opposition. Shurcliff debuted the Citizens League Against the Sonic Boom (CLASB) in March 1967 with a handful of friends and colleagues. Their mission was to eliminate the SST program and keep its boom out of American skies. By June, CLASB had about 230 members in 18 states. What united them, Shurcliff told The New York Times, was that they were “human beings who don’t like to be hit over our heads without our permission being asked.”.

In a recent development, SST opposition grew as the fight dragged on. Environmental groups joined in, along with economists who doubted the SST would ever pay for itself. For a man newly introduced to public relations, Shurcliff seized the moment, casting sonic booms in the language of a rising environmental movement, calling them “sonic pollution.” Atmospheric scientists began warning that SST’s high-altitude exhaust could erode the ozone layer.

In 1971, Congress finally voted to cut off the program’s funding, ending America’s bid for a supersonic passenger airliner. But across the Atlantic, the European program was forging ahead.

In a recent development, in 1963, a plane flew to space. Why couldn’t we go farther?

In 1934, Chrysler bet big on teardrop-shaped cars.

Robotaxis almost happened in 1964—with help from the U.S. government.

Recent findings suggest that in 1871, cities almost got moving sidewalks. Why are we still waiting?

During WWI, a daredevil pilot helped invent the first ‘drones’.

In 1916, hybrid cars could’ve changed history. But Ford wouldn’t allow it.

It has been revealed that concorde began carrying paying passengers in January 1976, cruising at twice the speed of sound and crossing the Atlantic in about three and a half hours. But the U.S. overland ban confined it mostly to ocean routes. Only British Airways and Air France, both state-owned at the time, ever flew Concorde’s small fleet.

In July 2000, an Air France Concorde flight crashed on takeoff outside Paris, killing everyone aboard and halting flights for more than a year. In February 2002, Popular Science writer Bill Sweetman called the crash not only a tragedy but also “a metaphor for the sorry state of supersonic air travel.” But he also reported that a latest supersonic race had “quietly” begun.

Private-jet maker Gulfstream wanted “a passenger jet for the rich that can smash the sound barrier yet is quiet enough to fly anywhere, anytime.” Controlling the boom was the chief obstacle. But in August 2003, over the California desert, a modified Northrop Grumman F-5 fighter plane demonstrated that a sonic boom could be reshaped and softened.

Two months later, Concorde made its last commercial flight, officially ending the supersonic era for passenger airliners.

It has been revealed that the modern darling of supersonic flight is NASA’s X-59, a one-seat research jet built by Lockheed Martin’s Skunk Works. With a tapered nose that stretches roughly a third of its length, the plane’s shape spreads the shock waves so they reach the ground as a thump rather than a boom. The X-59 first flew in October 2025, went supersonic in June 2026, and a week later reached its target of Mach 1.4, or roughly 925 mph at 55,000 feet. Next, NASA plans to fly it over U.S. communities and ask residents how the thumps sound to them. In effect, we’re gearing up for Oklahoma City again, six decades later, albeit, with a gentler jolt.

Recent findings suggest that since Concorde’s retirement, a handful of private supersonic startups have come, and mostly gone. Denver-based Boom Supersonic flew its one-third-scale XB-1 demonstrator faster than sound three times in January 2025, claiming that no audible boom reached the ground. Its engineering innovation is to exploit atmospheric physics. Since sound travels faster in warm air near the ground than in the frigid air up high, a jet flying only slightly faster than sound at altitude is effectively flying slower than sound near the surface. So its shock waves bend back upward before they land, a phenomenon called Mach cutoff. Boom’s planned Overture jet, seating 60 to 80 passengers, would cruise at Mach 1.7 over oceans—leaving booms in its wake—but just above Mach 1 over land, where their booms would never be heard on the ground, just the distant rumble of their jet engines. The plane hasn’t been built, and its engine is still in development.

But Washington isn’t waiting for the data. A June 2025 executive order directed the FAA to repeal its 1973 sonic boom ban over land. In July 2026, the agency proposed a replacement. Civilian jets, both commercial and private, could fly supersonic over U.S. soil as long as their booms register no more than 0.11 pounds per square foot on the ground, about a twentieth of Concorde’s. That’s about 5 Pa, or slightly less than the pressure felt standing next to the speakers at a live concert (6.5 Pa). But airlines, airports, and Europe’s aviation regulator have questioned whether enough evidence supports the number, which the FAA set without the X-59 having flown over a single community.

Even if the boom fades to a thump, the environmental cost doesn’t. Flying faster than sound means fighting far more drag. According to a 2018 analysis by the International Council on Clean Transportation, a fresh supersonic airliner would “burn five to seven times as much fuel per passenger as a comparable subsonic jet.” Boom Supersonic claims Overture will be able to run entirely on sustainable aviation fuel, but airlines, not manufacturers, decide what goes in the tank.

As Popular Science’s Bill Sweetman wrote in 2002, if you can afford a supersonic jet, “you’re not worried about a few lousy tons of fuel.” But everyone below will bear the cost of supersonic jetsetters’ small travel-time benefit in excess noise and climate-warming emissions.

Shurcliff saw this attempt to relax the rules coming. “Once they start flying, they’re going to want to fly them everywhere,” he told The Fresh York Times in 1967, warning that over-water routes would be “like a foot in the door.” Fifty-nine years later, thanks to the FAA, the door is swinging open. It’s up to us to decide whether we’re prepared to live with the repercussions or push back as Shurcliff did more than half a century ago.

In A Century in Motion, Popular Science revisits fascinating transportation stories from our archives, from hybrid cars to moving sidewalks, and explores how these inventions are re-emerging today in surprising ways.

The $33.94 million project in Fort Mill is expected to create 70 jobs, the South Carolina Department of Commerce confirmed Wednesday. It’ll be the Bolzano, Italy-based Alpitronic’s first operation in South Carolina, just across the state line from its North American headquarters in Charlotte.

The HYC400 packs up to 400 kW into a single unit. If you’ve stopped at an IONNA Rechargery, you may have already plugged into one.

In a recent development, the HYC1000 works differently. A separate power cabinet can send up to 1 MW across as many as eight vehicles at once, shifting power between them as their charging needs change. Operators can configure it with CCS or NACS plugs for passenger EVs or a Megawatt Charging System (MCS) plug for compatible heavy-duty trucks.

It has been revealed that alpitronic’s 400 kW chargers were already being made in Wisconsin for Mercedes-Benz High-Power Charging in 2024. Alpitronic Americas CEO Patrik Herrnegger said the Fort Mill plant “will put US production under our direct control, bring us closer to our customers, and enable us to serve them more efficiently.”.

Industry observers note that the 173,315-square-foot site at 3560 Stateview Blvd. (pictured above) will also house a testing lab, repair operations, a warehouse, logistics space, and offices. South Carolina approved job development credits and awarded York County a $200,000 grant to help pay for building improvements.

Tech Report: Taking Fish Oil to Boost Brain Health? A 2-Year Study Questions the Benefits

📅 29 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1051 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Healthline

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that A clinical trial found that taking high dose omega-3 supplements for 2 years did not help memory or thinking skills in older adults at increased risk of Alzheimer’s.Researchers at Keck Medicine of USC led the study, which was published in eBioMedicine.
  • Getting omega-3s from food or supplements is important since the body cannot make them.
  • Keck Medicine researchers enrolled 365 adults who did not have dementia, and whose ages ranged from 55 to 80, with an average age of 66.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that A clinical trial found that taking high dose omega-3 supplements for 2 years did not help memory or thinking skills in older adults at increased risk of Alzheimer’s.Researchers at Keck Medicine of USC led the study, which was published in eBioMedicine. Participants took either a daily high dose supplement of omega-3 fatty acid docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) or a placebo.Fish oil is one of the most familiar ways people get omega-3s. However, the supplement in this clinical trial wasn’t made from fish, Hussein Yassine, MD, director of the USC Center for Personalized Brain Health with Keck Medicine of USC and the study’s lead researcher, told Healthline. This article uses the broader term omega-3 supplements.The researchers found that taking supplements raised omega-3 levels in participants’ brains, yet it didn’t change their memory, thinking skills, or brain structure.Dung Trinh, MD, an internist at MemorialCare Medical Group and chief medical officer of Healthy Brain Clinic in Irvine, California, who wasn’t involved in the study, told Healthline that the findings challenge the common belief that omega-3 supplements, such as fish oil, can help prevent Alzheimer’s disease or improve memory.Millions of older adults take omega-3 supplements. In a 2017–2018 federal survey, 21.8% of U.S. adults age 60 and older reported taking an omega-3 fatty acid supplement in the past 30 days, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).

Getting omega-3s from food or supplements is important since the body cannot make them.

Keck Medicine researchers enrolled 365 adults who did not have dementia, and whose ages ranged from 55 to 80, with an average age of 66.

Recent findings suggest that subjects obtained little DHA from their diets and had at least one risk factor for dementia. Of the 365 people who enrolled, 225 completed the trial, according to the study. Nearly half (47%) carried APOE4.Participants took either 2,000 milligrams (mg) of DHA or a placebo every day. Neither participants nor researchers knew who received the supplement.

The supplement in the trial contained more than 90% DHA and about 1% EPA, Yassine said.

Researchers found that high dose omega-3 supplements raised DHA levels in the fluid around the brain and spinal cord by 17%.

In a recent development, both groups in the trial scored about the same on memory and thinking tests. Brain structure appeared the same in both groups.

Recent findings suggest that the supplement also raised omega-3 levels in the blood. Over two years, participants’ omega-3 index, a measure of EPA and DHA in red blood cells, rose from 4.9% to 11%.“That’s a massive increase, but that doesn’t translate into clinical outcomes,” Yassine stated.DHA reached the brain equally well in people with and without the gene variant APOE4, which is linked to a higher risk of Alzheimer’s disease, according to the study.Earlier trials couldn’t tell whether DHA failed to reach the brain or reached it without helping, the study’s authors say. This trial answers that open question, since the DHA got there.“This tells us that just because a supplement reaches the brain doesn’t necessarily mean it will improve brain function or prevent cognitive decline,” Trinh said.

Sources indicate that the lack of measurable change in memory and thinking may come down to how the body uses omega-3s, according to Yassine.He noted it’s “really important to distinguish between omega-3 metabolism and omega-3 supplements.”A supplement can raise omega-3 levels, yet the body may still break them down before they reach the right places. Obesity, smoking, and a lack of exercise can all reduce how much omega-3 gets into the brain, he said.

Some fish and fish oil supplements may offer more than omega-3s. These sources may also include other nutrients such as lutein, vitamin E, and selenium, Yassine stated.A supplement can raise the level, but if you don’t change the holistic program, just going and increasing the level by itself may not be sufficient,” he said.Researchers tend to fall into two camps on how to read the results, according to Yassine.

Some see the findings as evidence that supplements don’t work in isolation. Others argue the trial would need a longer follow-up or sicker participants to answer the question.Trinh pointed to the study’s length. “It’s also vital to recognize that Alzheimer’s disease develops over decades, so a two-year study may not be long enough to determine whether DHA supplementation has any long-term preventive benefits,” he noted.

Fish oil supplements contain two omega-3 fatty acids, eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA) and DHA, according to the National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health (NCCIH).

Foods such as fish and flaxseed also contain omega-3s, according to the National Institutes of Health’s Office of Dietary Supplements (ODS).Research suggests omega-3s may help reduce inflammation, support heart health, and promote childhood growth and development.

Some observational studies link diets high in omega-3s with a lower risk of cognitive decline and dementia.

Researchers say omega-3s may help preserve cognition by supporting brain cells in continuing to function and maintain their membranes, according to the ODS.“Omega-3s are important for the brain, and we and many others have shown that having higher levels of omega-3s is associated with less Alzheimer’s pathology, better cognition, and many other protective outcomes,” Yassine said, in contrast to the trial findings.Trinh agreed. “DHA plays an essential role in maintaining healthy brain cells, and there is evidence that eating fish as part of a healthy dietary pattern may support long-term brain health,” he said.Research on omega-3s and brain health is ongoing, and there is insufficient evidence to draw firm conclusions about their effectiveness.

Some people may still benefit from a supplement, according to Yassine, including:.

Some neurologists test omega-3 levels, though the test isn’t standard, Yassine remarked.People with nutritional deficiencies or certain genetic or metabolic traits may respond differently to omega-3 supplements, and researchers still need to learn who might benefit, Trinh said.

People who already take fish oil or other omega-3 supplements for other reasons, such as high triglycerides, should make those decisions with their healthcare professionals, he said.

Trinh remarked he tells his patients that “what is good for the heart is generally good for the brain.” He recommended the following healthy habits:.

“Overall, this study reminds us that there is no magic pill for preventing Alzheimer’s disease and that maintaining brain health requires a much broader approach,” Trinh mentioned.

#224603. Voyager 1 is officially one light-day away from Earth

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1032 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Popsci ↗ Open Full Page

Voyager 1 is officially one light-day away from Earth

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1032 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • After traveling through space for almost 50 years, NASA’s Voyager 1 spacecraft should be one light-day away from Earth.
  • William Kurth, a research scientist at the University of Iowa who has worked on the Voyager mission since 1974 tells Popular Science that this mission is about more than just science.
  • Recent findings suggest that “The Voyager missions represent humanity’s curiosity and hunger to understand our species’ place in the universe,” he indicates.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

After traveling through space for almost 50 years, NASA’s Voyager 1 spacecraft should be one light-day away from Earth. The probe reached this record-breaking milestone at approximately 5:16:07 a.m. EST on Wednesday, November 18. Since takes about 24 hours to receive any signal from Voyager 1, NASA officially confirmed that it reached the distance on Thursday, November 19.

William Kurth, a research scientist at the University of Iowa who has worked on the Voyager mission since 1974 tells Popular Science that this mission is about more than just science.

Recent findings suggest that “The Voyager missions represent humanity’s curiosity and hunger to understand our species’ place in the universe,” he indicates. “They show that we are explorers and can work together to do wonderful things.”.

Astronomers often describe vast cosmic distances in light-years. It’s arguably the most famous unit of measurement when talking about the universe, in part because of its sheer incomprehensibility. A single particle of light travels at a speed of about 186,282 miles per second. Hypothetically speaking, if you fired a beam of light into the night sky at the outset of reading this story, it would travel around 44.7 million miles into space by the time you finished.

But even a unit like a light-minute isn’t particularly useful to astronomers. For them, cosmic measurements only start making sense on a scale of light-years. Voyager 1 is nowhere close to a light-year away from Earth, but a light-day (approximately 16,094,799,105 miles) is still basically impossible to envision as a distance. And since radio communications travel at nearly the speed of light, any messages to and from the spacecraft will require about 24 (Earth) hours to receive.

“Voyager 1 crossing the light-day threshold is yet another historic feat on an extraordinary voyage of discovery,” Dave Gallagher, the director of NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory, stated in an emailed statement confirming the milestone. “Above all, this milestone stands as a testament to the exceptional teams who built, programmed, and fly these spacecraft today, and who have overcome countless challenges to keep them connected to Earth across the vastness of space. As NASA pushes toward latest frontiers in human and robotic exploration, Voyager and the people behind its success continue to inspire us to reach farther and dream bigger.”.

It has been revealed that even at one light-day from Earth, Voyager 1 isn’t done just yet. While several of its instruments are no longer functioning, it still routinely sends back invaluable information from its vantage point beyond the solar system.

“Voyager 1 is telling us about our sun’s interaction with its galactic neighborhood. It has told us about the amount of galactic cosmic rays, unfiltered by the sun’s magnetic field,” says Kurth. “We are learning about the variation of plasma density in the interstellar medium just outside the heliosphere (sun’s extended atmosphere). We’re anxious to see where the direction of the magnetic field rotates from one similar to the heliospheric direction to that of the pristine interstellar medium.”.

It has been revealed that “Though it might be a long shot, I hope to see Voyager 1 crossing into the predicted hot hydrogen wall,” Adam Szabo, a Project Investigator on Voyager’s Magnetometer Experiment, tells Popular Science. “The wall is composed of neutral hydrogen atoms, so it will not register easily, but it must have some magnetic and plasma wave signature.”.

Industry observers note that voyager 1 launched on September 5, 1977, heading for Jupiter and Saturn. Voyager 1 has 10 scientific instruments onboard, including two Golden Records engraved with sights, sounds, and depictions of life on Earth onboard—should the probe encounter any extraterrestrial life.

In a recent development, in March 1979, the Voyager 1 discovered a thin ring around Jupiter and two fresh Jovian moons: Thebe and Metis. When it reached Saturn in 1980, the spacecraft spotted five new moons and a new ring called the G-ring.

As part of a concept that NASA called the Grand Tour, the Voyager mission as a whole took advantage of a once-every-175-year alignment of the outer planets for a grand tour of the solar system. Its twin spacecraft Voyager 2 later explored Neptune and Uranus.

On February 17, 1998, Voyager 1 became the furthest human-made object in space, after overtaking NASA’s Pioneer 10 probe. It crossed into interstellar space in August 2012, and became the first spacecraft to cross the heliosphere. This boundary is where the influences from outside of our solar system are stronger than those from our sun.

Recent findings suggest that all good things must come to an end, of course. Voyager 1 is powered by three radioisotope thermoelectric generators (RTGs) fueled by decaying plutonium-23. The isotope possesses a 87.74-year half-life, so the batteries are currently operating at around two-thirds their original strength. NASA has slowly shut down onboard equipment in recent years to conserve energy, but there will come a time when there simply isn’t enough left in the RTGs for anything to operate. Barring any technical issues, mission engineers expect to bid Voyager 1 a final farewell sometime during the 2030s.

The spacecraft may cease its work as a cosmic laboratory, but its very existence ensures it will remain a monument to humanity’s potential as it barrels forward for eons.

Sources indicate that “Voyager 1 and its companion Voyager 2 have taught us time and again that nature is not as simple and predictable as we thought,” Kurth explains. “Voyager has always provided surprising differences from our best guesses as to what it will see in any upcoming region.”.

Additionally, Szabo adds that it has an important lesson for anyone on Earth who has ever had a dream.

“Do not be afraid to dream significant. In 1977, even the Grand Tour seemed like a long shot,” he indicates. “We did not even conceive of making it into interstellar space. Dream big.”.

#224601. I Didn't Get the “Letting Go” Memo

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1013 w)

I Didn't Get the “Letting Go” Memo

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1013 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 25, 2026 | Reviewed by Monica Vilhauer Ph.D.
  • Recent findings suggest that I never got a specific memo about how to let go of my children.
  • There is a well-worn path of letting go, which surprisingly begins when a child is a few hours old.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 25, 2026 | Reviewed by Monica Vilhauer Ph.D.

Recent findings suggest that I never got a specific memo about how to let go of my children. My parents, as Australians, were more open to this idea than the European parents of many of my contemporaries, most of whom had recently endured the trauma of the holocaust. But even with a different cultural background, I've felt that mothering and letting go is, on so many levels, a contradiction in terms. Mothers receive an intuitive message: You are meant to stay close to your children, to protect them, and to look after them. We assume this means always.

There is a well-worn path of letting go, which surprisingly begins when a child is a few hours old. Lisa Baraitser1 opened my mind to this in her description of the newborn falling asleep. It describes the mother’s response, her feelings and tears as she realizes that her infant’s “first sleeps” hold a deeper meaning as he/she goes “away on their own for the first time.” It’s almost like a jolt, an awareness for the mother that her infant, a mere few hours old, drifts in sleep to a place that she isn’t part of. In the full swing of post-birth, we aren’t really tuned into receiving this message.

This realization would have helped me. It would have informed my understanding of mothering: that one’s child, even at a few hours old, is a separate being. It's a startling and humbling recognition that, as mothers, we don't own our children; we are “there to be left,” as Erna Furman2 puts it.

We get these messages continually from our children. The child crawls away from us to experience the world, then walks, then goes to preschool. But for the first 11 or so years, we are the ultimate hands-on caregivers. We feed, rock, and change our infants. When they are toddlers and young children, we kiss their skinned knees, and we are at their service all day and during the night to calm their nightmares and their sore tummies. To them, mom is the person who knows how to fix things—everything. We are their person.

It has been revealed that this changes when our adolescent teenager surfaces. We become sparring partners, and if we are lucky, we get more than a contemptuous look or that stare. We return to nights of interrupted sleep, as we stay awake all hours waiting for them to come home. We spend a lot of time reflecting on and talking about what’s gotten hold of our child. Why is there no conversation? Why are they so abrupt and rude? Why is it all about their friends? It’s so difficult to reframe this as a process of healthy separation, a letting go, as they wear us out in a upcoming way— with emotional exhaustion. Those of us who want to hold onto the earlier status quo are in trouble.

It has been revealed that the teenage years give us pause for thought. How do we receive the message to back off, that we need to let go? One of the wisest comments that I ever heard about this stage is that a child is like this because he/she can be, because he/she has a mom who can bear it. The child intuits this through continual testing. It’s all part of the separation. It requires us to hold onto the sides of the roller coaster driven by our child, to stay on board and go with it while insisting on some guardrails, believing that our child will return to us one day, albeit in a different form.

According to recent reports, then, as our children approach late teens and early 20s, there are latest challenges and shifts as they hopefully enter the workforce, continue their education, train for a trade or technical career, or go out on his/her own. We become more like roommates on different programs as we navigate home life with another adult. Or they leave home.

Recent findings suggest that the next stage may include our child partnering, and the cycle begins again with their own children. Our next lesson is that it's their turn to make their own family. Are we able to watch and learn with curiosity and gratitude?

It has been revealed that as we look back at our mothering, it’s clear that one of the most important parts of mothering is to intuit when to let go and how: to know that each child is different, and to ask ourselves whether we've been adaptive, accepting, and understanding enough. Have we tried to hold on too long or let them go too soon? Have we used guilt, been a victim, or judged them openly and harshly? Have we encouraged our child at each stage to learn their own place in the world?

It has been revealed that how do we get there? Letting go of one’s children is an art form. It takes sensitivity, a lack of ego, and not putting ourselves first.

My work on ambivalence has guided my understanding of this. Mothering is full of contradictory feelings that can be difficult to bear, that often seize us at any one time, and also renew our love and give us the strength to separate.

Sources indicate that saying goodbye to our 4-year-old at preschool is a bittersweet love. We feel both fury that our 15-year-old arrives home at 4 am without calling and absolute love when he/she walks through the door in one piece. We feel pride and joy when we see our child commit to a partner, but also loss; they belong to someone else now. All of these feelings mean separation.

  • Sir Patrick Stewart, best-known for portraying Captain Jean-Luc Picard in “Star Trek” and Professor Charles Xavier in the “X-Men” film franchise, has died.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sir Patrick Stewart, best-known for portraying Captain Jean-Luc Picard in “Star Trek” and Professor Charles Xavier in the “X-Men” film franchise, has died. He was 86.

The legendary actor and thespian passed away on October 28 after a “brief and poignant journey with Alzheimer’s Disease and Lewy Body Dementia,” according to his longtime spokesperson, Kelly Bush Novak, in a statement to The Hollywood Reporter.

He died peacefully at his home in Los Angeles, where he was receiving care from his wife, Sunny Ozell.

“He has been held in the warm embrace of family and friends, surrounded by live music, prayer, tears, laughter and the kind of profound emotion that only he could inspire after a lifetime of devotion to us all,” Bush Novak wrote in the statement. “We will forever cherish the peaceful ease and reflection on his face, an enduring reminder of his invincible grace.”.

Stewart’s acting career spanned more than six decades across theater, television, and film.

A longtime member of the Royal Shakespeare Company, he rose to international fame in 1987 with “Star Trek: The Next Generation” and later became known for his portrayal of Professor Charles Xavier in the 2000 film “X-Men” and its numerous sequels.

He was knighted by Queen Elizabeth II in 2010 for his contributions to drama.

Alzheimer’s disease and Lewy body dementia are two progressive neurological conditions that can affect memory, thinking, behavior, and a person’s ability to perform everyday activities.

According to the National Institute on Aging (NIA), both conditions can cause dementia, a term used to describe a decline in cognitive abilities severe enough to interfere with daily life.

Alzheimer’s disease is the most common cause of dementia. The condition is associated with abnormal buildups of proteins called amyloid and tau in the brain, which disrupt communication between nerve cells and contribute to their damage.

According to recent reports, the NIA states that memory problems are often among the earliest symptoms of Alzheimer’s. As the disease progresses, people may experience increasing difficulty with language, reasoning, decision making, and recognizing familiar people.

Recent findings suggest that lewy body dementia, meanwhile, is associated with abnormal deposits of a protein called alpha-synuclein in the brain. These deposits, known as Lewy bodies, affect brain chemicals involved in thinking, movement, mood, and sleep, according to the NIA.

People with Lewy body dementia may experience changes in attention and alertness, visual hallucinations, muscle stiffness, difficulty walking, and sleep disturbances.

According to the Alzheimer’s Association, the two conditions may co-occur, and their overlapping symptoms may make diagnosis more challenging.

It has been revealed that currently, neither condition has a cure, but treatments are available to help manage symptoms. Certain medications can also slow cognitive decline in some people with early Alzheimer’s disease.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Recent findings suggest that GM indicates the pilot participants will be its first EV drivers in California to export power from their cars to their homes.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

GM Energy and WeaveGrid are launching a vehicle-to-grid (V2G) pilot that will let select Southern California Edison (SCE) customers send electricity from their EV batteries back to the grid. Eligible drivers could get more than $16,000 in help with equipment and installation, and earn money when the grid needs their power.

Recent findings suggest that GM indicates the pilot participants will be its first EV drivers in California to export power from their cars to their homes. Through the California Energy Commission, eligible customers in SCE’s Emergency Load Reduction Program can get up to $8,000 toward a GM Energy V2H system and up to $8,099 toward eligible installation costs, including connecting the system to the grid.

Chevy, GMC, and Cadillac EV drivers can use time-of-use energy management to take advantage of lower rates and may be paid for participating in eligible demand-response events. How much they save or earn depends on their rate blueprint, electricity use, and participation.

GM already offers managed charging through 13 utilities, and each program varies by utility.

An EV battery stores direct current (DC), and your house and the grid use alternating current (AC). GM’s current home backup system uses a wall-mounted inverter to convert the power. With AC bidirectional charging, the car’s onboard inverter does the job. Moving that work into the car could make the equipment on your garage wall simpler and cheaper to install.

Not in CA, but we use solar, time of use, and EVs to minimize our energy costs. We’re not feeding power back to the grid from our cars, but the combo of TOU, solar and EVs does allow us to reduce costs significantly. Solar covers all the expensive peak power, I have the cars start charging early enough to use any extra solar, and the rest is off peak at half cost.

GM is joining CharIN‘s North American AC V2G task force, which is working to align technical standards, equipment certification, and utility approval requirements. In Southern California, the pilot will give GM and its partners a look at how the process works for drivers, from signing up and getting the hardware installed to getting utility approval and sending power back.

Prickly pears can generate solar electricity

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (571 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that most plants rely on real-time photosynthesis for food, which means they aren’t generating energy unless the sun is out.
  • Plants generally absorb carbon dioxide through pores in their leaves, but the prickly pear can’t afford such an evolutionary luxury.
  • Environmental biologists certainly did.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that most plants rely on real-time photosynthesis for food, which means they aren’t generating energy unless the sun is out. Meanwhile, cacti like the prickly pear must get creative in order to survive the harsh conditions they live in. With high temperatures and little water, these plants and similar species like aloe and pineapple evolved a specialized process called crassulacean acid metabolism (CAM). The overall principles are the same, but instead of converting carbon dioxide (CO₂) and water into sugars solely during daylight, CAM allows a prickly pear to extend its photosynthesis over a full 24 hours.

Plants generally absorb carbon dioxide through pores in their leaves, but the prickly pear can’t afford such an evolutionary luxury. The desert heat would turn those same tiny openings into water drains. With CAM, a prickly pear only absorbs carbon dioxide at night, and subsequently turns it into malic acid. Photosynthesis later breaks down the acid—but only on the side of the plant directly exposed to sunlight. The shady side retains its malic acid, creating a pH concentration gradient. Interestingly, this pH imbalance is also one of the underlying principles for generating electricity…see where this is going?

Environmental biologists certainly did. In a study published today in the journal Plants, People, Planet, a team at the University of California, Santa Cruz, (UC Santa Cruz) detailed a new, interdisciplinary system that transforms the common prickly pear into a green solar panel. Although prickly pear voltages aren’t enough to deliver a noticeable jolt, they are strong enough to power the tiny sensors often used by farmers to monitor their crops. With some additional fine-tuning, their novel methods could offer a promising, sustainable adaptation to ongoing climate concerns.

“It was just so nice to have 10 students in a room from all across campus working together on a single project. When we’re looking at climate solutions, that’s what we need,” Charlie Chesney, a UC Santa Cruz environmental scientist and study co-author, stated in a statement.

Wiring a single spiky plant doesn’t do much, but linking them together adds up. As few as eight prickly pears are enough to generate 4.5 volts of electricity—nearly three times the charge of a commercial AA battery. That’s more than enough to power the common, low-energy sensors used to assess plants.

“There are many commercial applications of cacti [for] monitoring their health using a low-power system like ours, that is just operating off on the side and is self-powered,” explained UC Santa Cruz ecologist and study co-author Michael Loik.

He offered one such scenario, where wired prickly pears function as organic “sentinels” that monitor field conditions and relay the information back to a farmer’s office.

“This could be a really interesting avenue to pursue,” he added.

The idea isn’t limited to the prickly pear, either. Any plant that uses CAM—aloe, pineapple, agave—could benefit from a similar battery upgrade. The team even assessed how the cacti performed under a standard desert challenge like drought. Even after 15 months without water, sample prickly pears weren’t simply surviving—they were still photosynthesizing. In some cases, the resultant voltages were higher than watered control plants.

“This was a really surprising result, but also demonstrated how resilient a cactus is—it could still produce electricity even when it seems, to us, like it’s near death,” added Chesney.

NHL may not be a household name, but its all-newly introduced, all-electric NTE240E ultra-class haul track could change that with a 240 ton payload, over 4.1 MWh of battery, advanced regenerative braking, and a world’s first double-gun MCS charging setup.

For the uninitiated, Inner Mongolia North Hauler Joint Stock Co., Ltd. (NHL) is a Chinese heavy equipment manufacturer specializing in the enormous rigid-frame haul trucks used in open-pit mining operations. Established in 1988, NHL has decades of experience building mining trucks for customers around the world, including some of the industry’s largest diesel-electric hybrids. The brand’s new NTE240E is different, representing a firm’s real push into battery-electric mining equipment, and it’s powering that push with some seriously ambitious technology.

Let’s start with the battery. The NTE240E packs an absolutely MASSIVE battery pack, with the highest-capacity versions offering up to 4,100 kWh (4.1 MWh) of onboard energy storage. Keeping that much battery topped off is no small task, which is why NHL developed an equally ambitious energy replenishment strategy supporting dual-gun MCS charging, allowing its town-sized battery to go from 20% to 90% in under an hour.

That means operators can take advantage of shift changes and scheduled rest breaks to top off the battery without sacrificing an entire work shift to charging – but even more impressive than the fact that all that juice can be crammed into so major a battery in so little time is the fact that, according to NHL, it can be done at just 25°C (about 77°F).

Industry observers note that plugging in isn’t the only way the NTE240E drinks its juice. NHL’s fresh dynamic power reception system uses overhead current collectors to supply electricity directly to the truck while it’s climbing loaded mine roads, allowing it to then “ride the brakes” for more energy all the way downhill.

In a recent development, the combined technologies allow NHL’s operators to keep the massive trucks moving without relying entirely on their onboard batteries. The result is a claimed 15% improvement in energy efficiency over the ultra-class industry average.

Sources indicate that that efficiency turns into savings, which means the economics of running an NTE240E could be just as compelling as the emissions savings – and those are substantial. NHL says each NTE240E can reduce harmful carbon emissions by more than 2,000 tons annually, even as it cuts operating costs by more than 60% compared to a comparably capable diesel.

According to recent reports, what’s more, because the massive BEV’s electrical system eliminates the need for engine-related hardware like generators and the maintenance and overhaul costs associated with those components. Taken as a whole, the NHL seems to be a compelling offering … but that’s not for me to say. You guys are the experts – let us know what you think of the upcoming NHL NTE240E, in the comments.
