The Courage to Question Our Own Certainty

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (737 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 25, 2026 | Reviewed by Monica Vilhauer Ph.D.
  • In a recent development, there are a plethora of potentially polarizing complications these days in all aspects of our lives!
  • Our positioning and decisions on an issue seem like they happen in the blink of an eye.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 25, 2026 | Reviewed by Monica Vilhauer Ph.D.

In a recent development, there are a plethora of potentially polarizing complications these days in all aspects of our lives! It seems that we can hardly get a point of view on the table before a fellow conversationalist debunks our idea and discredits us along the way. Take your pick from a bushel full of igniting issues, whether it be global warming, wars, increasing the tax percentage for the very wealthy, or the strengths and weaknesses of our favorite political personalities; there will be no shortage of strong opinions. You can also be assured that before the full set of points of view are exposed or explored, one or more folks will have already decided what the correct point of view should be.

Our positioning and decisions on an issue seem like they happen in the blink of an eye. This instant judgement can create ill will, stress for us and the other, and can challenge or ruin long-standing relationships. Furthermore, it will likely lead to a suboptimal exploration and resolution of the salient points of view. The pivot that I would like to explore is realizing that although our interpretations and positions usually feel quite certain to us, they most likely do not represent the whole of the reality of that situation; they are a narrower, biased slice of the problem or solution.

In a recent development, I would like to explore what can happen when we can loosen our grip on our story/point of view, and instead consider what might ensue if we instead question our own certainty. This, of course, would require slowing down enough to really listen first and then explore the fuller reality of the situation together; then, with skillful listening and openness to other ways of thinking, we can have a meaningful and civil dialogue.

Sources indicate that we seem to be experiencing a plethora of fractured conversations, competing accounts of the truth, information overload, and fear about the future, all of which are leading to what we might call “contemporary exhaustion.” And if the impact of this on us personally wasn’t enough, the relational tension as well as the societal and political challenges are at an all-time high. It is so much more likely that answers to our difficult questions will land somewhere in the middle of the two opposing extremes being debated, or in a yet-to-be-discovered “third alternative” idea that cannot possibly be uncovered because of the anger, tension, and lack of listening in the interchange. Just to ground this idea in one statistic: the American Psychological Association's Stress in America survey, "A Crisis of Connection," reported that 62% of adults considered societal divisions a significant stressor in their lives.

If you are willing to have the “courage to suspend the certainty” of your initial interpretation and allow for more information, thoughts, and feelings to emerge between you and another, amazing things can happen. Try following a simple practice of what I will call “thoughtful receptivity” using these 4 steps. Imagine that, before you know it, you are in a polarizing conversation with challenging points of view and heated feelings emerging. Each side draws his/her sword, and the point-counterpoint debate begins. You have enough presence to realize you are in the battle, and it likely will not end well. You feel triggered and notice the same for the other person. You remember this practice and do the following:.

Sources indicate that we all have the tendency to confuse the story we have crafted and are trying to tell with the whole truth about a situation. Perhaps a better way to proceed is to remain open to what we have not yet explored or understood, remain open to another way of thinking about a situation, and remain open to the other person. If we could find the grace to do so, we might learn to see and understand more deeply before we judge. All of this ultimately requires that we develop the courage to question our own certainty. If we could do so, it is very likely that our world would become a much better, kinder place to live and thrive.

According to recent reports, american Psychological Association. (2025). Stress in America 2025: A crisis of connection. https://www.apa.org/pubs/reports/stress-in-america/2025.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that one of the most common questions asked by first-time EV buyers is about the cost of electricity. Whether they plan to charge at home or find charging in the wild, everyone wants to know what to expect when it comes time to top off their batteries. One EV owner did the math after two months of EV ownership and came up with a surprising number: $7 a month.

Sources indicate that whether we’re talking gasoline, diesel, or electricity, one driver’s fuel costs can look dramatically different from another’s. How far they drive, how often, and under what conditions can matter just as much as what they drive. And while EVs may offer the greatest benefits to rural drivers covering long distances, a Redditor going by Suitable-Truth-350 took a different approach, moving into a highly walkable city for the express purpose of driving as little as possible.

“My wife and I recently retired and moved from a car dependent, rural/suburban area to a large, walkable city with good light rail. Our goal was to drive as little as possible,” write Suitable-Truth-350. “We took delivery of an Ioniq5 in August. We still have a daily walking life, but we use the car to see friends in the country, shop or travel around the greater Chicagoland area. After 2 months, we finally charged it.”.

Recent findings suggest that the result? Suitable states it took less than 30 minutes to juice their Ioniq 5 back up to an 80% SOC, at a total cost of $13.

“Driving the car is a pleasure,” they continue. “The pickup and smooth operation so different from our last ICE vehicle. First impression, we love the car and could never imagine going back to (a gasoline-powered car).”.

I’ve been saying it for years: drive an EV for a week and whatever range anxiety you might experience will disappear. And, while it seems like Suitable-Truth-350 didn’t have much range anxiety to begin with, it’s worth noting here that their situation isn’t that rare.

In their most recent national survey, AAA found that the average US driver covered less than 29 miles per day, with the vast majority weekly commuting totals falling well within the range of even the most affordable used EVs.

The same survey found that just 30% of Americans reported taking at least one road trip the previous summer, with an average one-way trip length of ~235 miles.

That 235 mile trip might be too much for a car like the Fiat 500e, but even that car – the upcoming EV with the shortest EPA-estimated range you can buy in the US – can make a 235 mile trip with a single 30-minute stop to charge. And in 2026 and 2027, they’re sure to find plenty of places to charge, thanks to a public charging network that’s newer, faster, and far more built out than they probably think, with more fast-charging locations opening every week and modern charging speeds that make longer stops the exception instead of the norm.

Recent findings suggest that our two EVs raised our monthly electric bill by ~ $60/mo. and that's without solar. That wouldn't have paid for one gas fill-up for a week in our previous gas cars. I don't think this is even a question. If you can charge at home, it's cheaper. If you rely on public charging all the time then it's a mixed bag but still generally cheaper in most parts of the country. All said, we have three EVs now and my monthly electric bill for our entire house with six people is less than what we paid for fuel in one gas car.

In other words: your charging costs are probably going to be higher than Suitable-Truth-350’s seven-ish dollars per month, but with $4/gallon premium and $6/gallon diesel still very much the norm in 2026, it’ll probably be less than you think, too.

Industry News: Healthier Salt Substitute May Prevent Millions of Deaths From Heart Disease

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A simple swap for salt could spare millions of cardiovascular disease-related deaths, new research suggests.
  • In a study published in Nature Health on November 4, researchers at The George Institute for Global Health modeled the potential impact of 193 countries switching from regular table salt to potassium-enriched salt.
  • They found the switch could prevent nearly 3 million deaths and more than 10 million new cases of heart and kidney disease worldwide each year.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A simple swap for salt could spare millions of cardiovascular disease-related deaths, new research suggests.

In a study published in Nature Health on November 4, researchers at The George Institute for Global Health modeled the potential impact of 193 countries switching from regular table salt to potassium-enriched salt.

They found the switch could prevent nearly 3 million deaths and more than 10 million new cases of heart and kidney disease worldwide each year.

In the United States, this simple salt swap could prevent nearly 105,000 deaths and about 492,000 new cases a year, the researchers estimated.

Industry observers note that about 130.6 million U.S. adults have cardiovascular disease, according to the American Heart Association (AHA).

Liping Huang, PhD, a senior data analyst in the Food Policy Division at The George Institute for Global Health and co-lead author of the study, told Healthline the team started with current blood pressure levels by sex, age, and country.

The researchers then estimated how replacing all salt with a salt substitute would change people’s sodium and potassium intake, blood pressure, and disease risk, she stated.The team modeled a blend of 75% sodium chloride and 25% potassium chloride. The study estimated these yearly results worldwide:.

The authors wrote that the model relied on data from a few years ago and on many assumptions, and that any large-scale switch would take years.

Potassium-enriched salt replaces some of the sodium chloride in regular table salt with potassium chloride, according to The George Institute.Asked where other salts like kosher salt and sea salt fit in, Huang stated those salts may contain some trace elements “which has those health halos around them, but essentially they’re still primarily sodium chloride.”Huang noted that potassium-enriched salt tastes “about the same as a regular table salt.” She said it’s possible a small number of people with a sensitive palate could taste a difference.

Industry observers note that huang stated that “it’s really hard for people to cut back their salt intake.”“But the easier way is just to replace part of the sodium chloride in our normal salt with potassium chloride, because increasing potassium intake also helps to reduce blood pressure,” she said.The two minerals play opposite roles in the body, according to Cheng-Han Chen, MD, a board certified interventional cardiologist and medical director of the Structural Heart Program at MemorialCare Saddleback Medical Center in Laguna Hills, CA. Chen wasn’t involved in the study.

“While sodium causes water retention and increased blood pressure, potassium will help the kidneys remove sodium from the body and lower blood pressure,” Chen told Healthline.Huang said she worked on an earlier trial of about 21,000 people in 600 rural villages in northern China in 2021.

People who used potassium-enriched salt had a 14% lower risk of stroke, a 13% lower risk of cardiovascular events, and a 12% lower risk of early death than those who used regular salt, according to a 2021 study in The Upcoming England Journal of Medicine that summarized the trial’s results.

The World Health Organization (WHO) endorsed potassium-enriched salt in a 2025 guideline, saying it can reduce blood pressure and the risk of cardiovascular disease.

Sources indicate that the AHA said potassium-based salt substitutes can help lower blood pressure in some adults. The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) issued labeling guidance in 2020 allowing an alternate name for potassium chloride on ingredient labels to include the word “salt.”“We think that blood pressure begins to improve as soon as 1 week after cutting back on sodium intake. The full benefit typically takes up to 4 weeks,” Chen said.

“We generally recommend a daily sodium limit of 2,300 milligrams (mg), ideally under 1,500 mg a day. Most people consume over 3,000 mg of sodium a day, well above the recommended limit,” Chen stated.The WHO recommends less than 2,000 mg of sodium per day and suggests at least 3,510 mg of potassium a day.In the United States, more than 70% of salt intake comes from processed and restaurant foods, according to the AHA.

It has been revealed that huang said that some people with advanced chronic kidney disease should avoid potassium-enriched salt.When the kidneys don’t work well, the body may not clear extra potassium efficiently, she said. That can lead to hyperkalemia, or high potassium levels in the blood, which can raise the risk of cardiac arrest, Huang said.Among people with stage 3 to stage 5 kidney disease, switching to salt substitutes could prevent about 750,000 deaths a year by lowering blood pressure and cause about 100,000 deaths a year from hyperkalemia, the researchers estimated.The AHA said that people with kidney disease or who take medications that affect potassium should check with a healthcare professional before using these products.

Sources indicate that an estimated 37 million U.S. adults have chronic kidney disease, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).

In a recent development, potassium-enriched salt is available at supermarkets in the U.S. Many major U.S. grocery chains, including Kroger, Walmart, and Publix, carry two types of products, according to their websites:.

Potassium-enriched salt typically costs about twice as much as regular salt, according to the study.Huang noted she hoped people would see the results and start thinking of the switch as “a simple thing I can do for their own health.”.

Recent findings suggest that did Max Verstappen like the Las Vegas Grand Prix that he dominated on Saturday night, as a racer? No.

The four-time champion under the former regulations continues to be outspoken about his judgment of F1’s current ‘nimble’ car regulations, which put more weight on battery management in the 50/50 hybrid system than on racing itself.

From the cockpit, Verstappen took the lead into the opening corner and managed his race from there.

When asked if he remembered the last time he won a race with the field so close, with so much jockeying for position, Verstappen almost caught himself before delivering the headline for this article and countless more.

Industry observers note that “I probably shouldn’t say it; I probably should not,” Verstappen started in the press conference. “I remember winning one like this when I was playing on Mario Kart.

“Sometimes, you drop back, and you get drafted, and there’s catch-up, always; when you drop back, you go faster.

“That’s the last time I felt something like this, Verstappen finished.

What was, from the outside, a thrilling race, where the field was able to play cat-and-mouse with Verstappen, make up ground, and pass, was for the leader not even enough to raise his heart rate.

Industry observers note that this was Verstappen’s fourth win in six races after a slow start for Red Bull and their new Ford Power Units. A change of tides to be proud of, even in a race that didn’t spark joy for the racer.

“When I look at it from my racer heart, no,” Verstappen answered when asked if he enjoyed the ‘crazy racing’ of the GP.

In a recent development, “When you look at it as a show, a spectacle, yes. I’ve enjoyed my repasting and everything, but I prefer to look at it with my racing heart, and no.

Even my heart rate- I was not nervous at all. It felt kinda cruising out there. Just try to press the battery whenever it was passing or to defend. But for the show, when you look at it from the outside, you probably like it.

Verstappen has elected not to take part in the latest Whoop F1 partnership that would show fans a driver's heart rate throughout the race.

Lando Norris, who finished second after spending the first half of the race outside the points, felt similar to Verstappen about the focus of the race, saying he paid more attention to energy deployment than what was actually in front of him.

According to recent reports, “The whole race was judging the battery the whole time,” Norris remarked. “I was looking at the battery more than I’m looking where I’m going around this track.”.

If you’ve been paying any attention to the shooter market these past few months, you won’t be surprised to learn that Battlefield 6 has been an unprecedented success for EA, and the Battlefield series as a whole.

The game managed to sell over 7 million units at launch, climbing to the top of the charts anywhere you look, including setting new series concurrent player records on Steam. Thanks to new data, we now better understand the true scale of this launch.

The latest Circana report, which looks at game and hardware sales in the United States, has arrived. This iteration covers the month of October, which is when Battlefield 6 was released.

It has been revealed that battlefield 6 was the top-selling game across all platforms during October - which isn’t surprising. It has overtaken NBA 2K26 to become 2025’s best-selling game year-to-date, making it the best-selling Battlefield game ever.

In October alone, the game sold more than the lifetime sales of Battlefield 1, previously the best-selling entry in the franchise.

Battlefield 6 even set records beyond just its own series, having now produced the highest single-month dollar sales (physical and digital) total for any full game released in the last three years. The previous record holder was 2022’s Modern Warfare 2.

November’s report, which is set to arrive midway through December, will show, once and for all, whether Battlefield 6 has been able to overtake Black Ops 7. With one exception, Call of Duty games have, for more than a decade, topped the best-selling year-to-date chart. Regardless of the quality of the individual titles, or the competition in any given year, nothing has been able to shake that dominance.

Given all this momentum, Battlefield 6 has a shot at dethroning Call of Duty this year, beating Black Ops 7 to become the year’s best-seller. You never want to count out the sheer popularity of Call of Duty among casual players, however, which is what’s going to make December’s report all the more interesting.

#224508. Breaking: Should Scientists Ignore Philosophers of Science?

Breaking: Should Scientists Ignore Philosophers of Science?

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (946 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 26, 2026 | Reviewed by Kaja Perina.
  • Sources indicate that the eminent evolutionary biologist and modeller John Maynard Smith was once asked about Karl Popper and the philosophy of science.
  • Sources indicate that this is why I've recently published an academic article on the topic.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 26, 2026 | Reviewed by Kaja Perina.

Sources indicate that the eminent evolutionary biologist and modeller John Maynard Smith was once asked about Karl Popper and the philosophy of science. His answer was not flattering. His impression was that scientists who take the philosophy of science seriously, and allow their research to be influenced by philosophical preconceptions, are "far more likely to do themselves harm than good". He loved reading philosophy of science and was always ready to argue about it, he added, but he did not believe that one should allow oneself to be influenced by it when actually thinking about science.

Sources indicate that this is why I've recently published an academic article on the topic. These are quite radical words, and though Maynard Smith's generalisation is untenable, there is an crucial insight to be extracted.

If modellers approach the philosophical literature on models with the goal of figuring out what models are and what a good model is, they might easily find themselves lured into naive monistic views of models that fail to represent the full epistemic richness of modelling practices, thereby turning them into worse scientists than they could have otherwise been.

This could happen in several ways. For instance, models with epistemic functions not recognised by narrow monist accounts might be discarded. Consider, for example, models with weak predictive power, but great generality and insight into complex systems.

Industry observers note that perhaps Maynard Smith's worry is most strongly illustrated in economics, where Milton Friedman and Karl Popper are taken to have the "last word" in any methodological debate, and are frequently invoked to both defend and criticise the work of modellers. They are perhaps paradigm cases of monist thinking. Friedman argued that the only relevant desideratum in science concerns predictive power, while Popper argued that what matters is falsifiability.

These accounts of science have received extensive criticism over the last decades. Indeed, the philosopher Alex Rosenberg argued that Friedman's naive picture single-handedly justified the existence of philosophy of economics as a distinct profession. Economists, however, are unlikely to read much if any work on methodology beyond Friedman and Popper. As the economist Dani Rodrik notes, economic methodology is relegated to specialised journals and, more importantly, is not really being taught in graduate school.

The result is that economists seem to believe that their science operates according to a simple form of falsificationism, a picture of science that, most contemporary philosophers of science would agree, both misrepresents scientific practice and provides the wrong ideal of how science ought to function.

The obvious counter to Maynard Smith's concern is that it is not an argument against the philosophy of science, but rather against bad philosophy of science, which limits, rather than fosters, insights into the richness of the epistemic tools available to scientists.

Philosophers are not innocent here. Some debates in the philosophy of science rest on such monist motivations to seek univocal accounts of laws, explanation, species, functions, preferences, and many more. As Peter Godfrey-Smith emphasised, one of the hazards of philosophy is the temptation to come up with theories that are "too broad and sweeping". This hazard has not been avoided in the philosophical literature on models. Many philosophers of science seem to be under the impression that once we figure out what "models" are and how they work, we can finally get a handle on all the other pressing questions in the philosophy of science. I argue that this way of thinking about models is grounded in a mistake.

According to recent reports, A philosophy of science worth reading takes the plurality, diversity, and richness of models and modelling practices seriously. It does not hand scientists a single criterion for good science.

According to recent reports, economists, Rodrik argues, need a better story about the kind of science they practise, and some economists have recently engaged with philosophical questions themselves, seeking contact with philosophers of economics in the process. Philosophers of science, in turn, should turn more of their attention toward both the social sciences and the philosophy of the social sciences. Their lack of engagement with this rich literature is a historical omission that may have provided a misguided understanding of how science works.

According to recent reports, should scientists ignore philosophers? They should ignore those who tell them that there is only one way of doing science well.

The Australian surfer-turned-DJ FISHER took an early lead and controlled the pace of the LEGO race, much like his Red Bull Racing counterpart did in the weekend’s Grand Prix.

Eleven stars represented one of the current F1 teams on the grid in their own Lego minicars.

FISHER was one of the 11 celebrities tasked with piloting a fully functional Lego minicar around the FIA-rated street circuit of Las Vegas, along with the likes of actors Hannah Waddingham, Brendan Hunt, Caleb McLaughlin, Jack Whitehall and Terry Crews, singer LISA, gold-medal gymnast Jordon Chiles, chef Gordon Ramsay, a Magician named Dynamo and fellow DJ Carl Cox.

Michelin Star-holding Ramsay was the first celebrity to be caught chatting, reaching out to grab LISA’s Ferrari-sponsored Lego minicar in hopes of regaining his position.

In the end, FISHER shared the podium with Chiles and Waddingham as the trio collected their comically oversized Lego trophies in gold, silver, and bronze.

A replay of the race can be watched on YouTube.

  • Sources indicate that black Budget is described as a “tactical” extraction shooter.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, you’d be forgiven for not remembering PUBG: Black Budget, the extraction off-shoot of the original battle royale shooter, PUBG. Black Budget has been sort of floating around the internet for months, but Krafton never really committed to revealing core details about the game, or when players will actually get to play it.

This changes today, as the publisher - along with the game’s developer, PUBG Studios, have finally lifted the lid off the upcoming shooter.

Sources indicate that black Budget is described as a “tactical” extraction shooter. Squads of players infiltrate a mysterious island trapped in a time loop. There’s a bit of a STALKER element here with anomalies and various, unpredictable environmental shifts.

Industry observers note that coli, the island in question, hides a research facility that holds secrets and artefacts, which is what players will be attempting to extract. This is very much a PvPvE shooter, though PUBG Studios says the focus will be on exploration and discovery, rather than constant combat.

The game’s first set of closed alpha tests is set for December. The first takes place December 12-14, and another is scheduled for December 19-21. That’s six days across two weeks, with the test only being available on PC. Both sessions will be open to players in North America, Europe, and Asia.

Recent findings suggest that as it usually works with these sorts of tets on Steam, the game’s Steam page has a link where you can request access. If granted, you’ll be able to find the closed alpha in your library and download it when the time comes.

Though this is a closed test, Krafton confirmed that players will be able to capture and livestream their gameplay. In fact, watching content creators might be how you get access, as Black Budget is going to have a Twitch Drops event running alongside those sessions.

When I played Arc Raiders prior to its launch, I likened its tense and uncertain atmosphere to that of the early days of PUBG, so it’s going to be very interesting to see what actual PUBG does with the extraction shooter premise.

So far, it sounds like it’s going to be doing its own thing, leaning more into the adventure side of the subgenre, but we’ll have to see how it all shakes out when the tests start. Indeed, the BR-like constantly shrinking circle sounds like it could be a game-changing twist.

#224505. Is Conspiracy Thinking in the Person or the Place?

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1310 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Psychologytoday ↗ Open Full Page

Is Conspiracy Thinking in the Person or the Place?

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1310 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Food should be chosen based on each person's blood group.
  • Evidence of alien contact is being concealed from the public.
  • These seem to have little in common, but people who agree with one tend to agree with the others (Lobato and colleagues, 2014).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 26, 2026 | Reviewed by Lybi Ma.

Here are three statements. How much do you agree with each?

Food should be chosen based on each person's blood group.

Evidence of alien contact is being concealed from the public.

These seem to have little in common, but people who agree with one tend to agree with the others (Lobato and colleagues, 2014).

All three statements come from questionnaires that measure what researchers call epistemically suspect beliefs: confident claims about how the world works that go beyond, or against, the available evidence.

Because these beliefs hang together so well, many researchers treat them as something close to a personality trait, a stable way of seeing things. Others see them as a response to the world. Conspiracy theories, for example, tend to spread during periods of social crisis (van Prooijen and Douglas, 2017).

If these beliefs are traits, they should stay roughly the same from year to year, regardless of what happens around a person. A response to the world would instead rise and fall as people’s view of that world changes. Most studies cannot tell which is true, because they measure people only once.

In a paper just published in Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin, my colleagues and I tested the two views (Alper and colleagues, 2026). The project, led by Sinan Alper of Yaşar University. was funded by TÜBİTAK, Türkiye's national science agency.

In a recent development, we surveyed the same adults in Türkiye and the United Kingdom five times, once every six months. At the start, 2,077 people participated in Türkiye and 959 in the UK. Each time, they reported these beliefs and rated corruption among public officials, business executives, and the media, as well as other attitudes.

It has been revealed that the two countries differ sharply on corruption. On Transparency International’s (2026) Corruption Perceptions Index, the UK ranks 20th of 182 countries, and Türkiye ranks 124th.

The three beliefs moved together.

In a recent development, on average, the beliefs declined slightly over the two years, except for conspiracy belief in Türkiye, which revealed no clear change. I wouldn't read much into this, since answering the same questions repeatedly can itself lower scores. What struck me more was how tightly linked the three beliefs were. At the start, the correlations between them were strong, ranging from .65 to .86. Change was linked even more tightly. When a person’s belief in the paranormal fell, their belief in pseudoscience and conspiracy theories tended to fall with it.

Recent findings suggest that one possibility is that all three reflect a single underlying tendency. Simpler explanations, such as people answering the survey less carefully over time, cannot yet be ruled out. Either way, much of the change is shared, but not all of it.

In Türkiye, people who saw more corruption over the past two years also became more open to conspiracy theories. Their paranormal and pseudoscientific beliefs did not follow. In the UK, we found no such link.

It has been revealed that this may seem to clash with the previous section, and in part it does. Most of the change in these beliefs is shared, but each may keep some room to move on its own. In Türkiye, corruption may have tracked the portion attributable to conspiracy beliefs alone. It makes sense that belief in conspiracy was the one to move. A conspiracy theory claims that powerful people are secretly working together for their own gain. Corruption is often a true version of that story. Black cats and blood-type diets have nothing to do with it.

At the start of the study, though, the link between perceived corruption and conspiracy belief was about twice as strong in the UK (r = .61) as in Türkiye (r = .32). The difference may come down to how common corruption is. Where it is relatively rare, seeing it everywhere may say more about the person than about the country and may function as a stable trait. Where corruption is widespread and changing, people’s sense of it may follow those changes, and conspiracy beliefs may shift accordingly.

Our answer is both. These beliefs are steady and hang together, but they can still change.

In a recent development, some factors seem to set a person’s starting point. People higher in authoritarianism, who value discipline and following leaders in unity, endorsed all three kinds of beliefs more in both countries. But changes in authoritarianism did not track changes in belief. Perceived corruption works differently, and whether it moves these beliefs seems to depend on where you live.

This fits earlier work. Conspiracy beliefs are more common in countries with widespread corruption and in less stable societies, where education offers less protection against them (Alper, 2023). In another study I coauthored, education was also less tied to trust in science in highly corrupt countries (Alper and colleagues, 2024). In such places, people might learn to distrust authority from experience.

When someone you know shares a conspiracy theory, ask two questions. Is this how they see everything, from health advice to the evening news? Or is it a response to something they have watched go wrong? The first kind of belief tends to change slowly. The second should be taken seriously, because sometimes suspicion points at something real.

It has been revealed that careful thinking still matters. In a recent experiment, my colleagues and I found that training designed to encourage reflection lowered conspiracy beliefs (Bayrak and colleagues, 2025). But when institutions keep giving people reasons to be suspicious, better thinking can only do so much. I guess that in some places the best answer to conspiracy thinking is institutions that give people less to suspect. Survey data like ours cannot settle that.

According to recent reports, sinan Alper and I have begun to test it experimentally. In two preregistered studies with nationally representative US samples, we described an unnamed US state or a fictional country as either highly corrupt or very clean (Alper and Yilmaz, 2026).

People found conspiracy claims about the corrupt place far more believable, and this was most closely tied to a sense that resources were being shared unfairly. The paper is still under peer review, and I will write about it once it is done.

Energy Drinks, Stimulant Supplements Linked to Higher Heart Risks in Young Adults

📅 04 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1377 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Healthline

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Latest research suggests that caffeinated energy drinks and stimulant supplements are associated with significantly higher risks of serious heart problems, including cardiac arrest and heart attack in young adults.
  • The findings, to be presented at the American Heart Association (AHA) Scientific Sessions 2026 November 6–9 in Chicago, are preliminary and can’t prove that energy drinks cause heart problems.
  • Still, the results highlight concerning cardiovascular effects of these popular products, particularly among adults under 35 who consume them regularly.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Latest research suggests that caffeinated energy drinks and stimulant supplements are associated with significantly higher risks of serious heart problems, including cardiac arrest and heart attack in young adults.

The findings, to be presented at the American Heart Association (AHA) Scientific Sessions 2026 November 6–9 in Chicago, are preliminary and can’t prove that energy drinks cause heart problems.

Still, the results highlight concerning cardiovascular effects of these popular products, particularly among adults under 35 who consume them regularly.

“These products are marketed as everyday pick-me-ups and sold next to soda and bottled water, so most people assume they carry no real risk,” study author Sai Samayamanthula, a fourth-year medical student at the University of Virginia School of Medicine in Charlottesville, VA, said in a news release.

“For many healthy people, if these products are consumed occasionally, the risk is probably small. However, individuals who consume energy drinks or other stimulant-containing supplements regularly can promptly exceed the recommended daily limit for caffeine, so it’s notable for people to know that there may be a risk of cardiovascular harm with these products,” Samayamanthula continued.

Researchers from the University of Virginia School of Medicine analyzed 28,345 reports submitted to the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) between 2017 and 2025.

Of these, 854 involved caffeinated energy drinks or stimulant supplements, while the remaining reports involved non-stimulant products.

Sources indicate that compared with non-stimulant products, cardiac arrest was reported approximately 11 times more often with energy drinks and stimulant supplements. Heart attacks were reported 4.5 times more often, while ventricular arrhythmias and palpitations were reported about four times more frequently.

Nearly 45% of heart-related reports involved adults ages 18 to 34.

In a recent development, “Our findings support the case for more systematic safety monitoring of caffeine- and stimulant-containing products. In addition, healthcare professionals should remember to ask their younger patients who have palpitations, chest pain or fainting spells if they recently or regularly consume these products,” Samayamanthula stated.

Industry observers note that gregory M. Marcus, MD, professor of medicine at the University of California, San Francisco School of Medicine, and chair of the 2026 AHA scientific statement on caffeine and cardiovascular disease, wasn’t involved in the study, but said the research “raises concerns that products with very high amounts of caffeine may be harmful to the cardiovascular system.”.

“Although there are biological reasons why that connection could be possible, the study does not prove that caffeine products cause these events, because other factors may have influenced the results found in this analysis,” Marcus mentioned in a news release.

“More research is needed to understand whether these stimulant products are truly responsible for the reported heart-related events.”.

Sources indicate that cheng-Han Chen, MD, board certified interventional cardiologist and medical director of the Structural Heart Program at MemorialCare Saddleback Medical Center in Laguna Hills, CA, said the findings, although concerning, are not surprising. Chen wasn’t involved in the study.

“We know that energy drinks can have significant effects on the cardiovascular system, primarily because of their stimulant properties,” he told Healthline.

Recent findings suggest that “Caffeine can increase blood pressure and heart rate, while other ingredients, such as guarana and taurine, may further contribute to cardiovascular stimulation and increased stress hormone levels. What is particularly concerning is the potential for these products to trigger serious complications, including abnormal heart rhythms, especially in people with underlying cardiovascular conditions.”.

Chen agreed that occasional energy drink consumption is unlikely to have long-term consequences for heart health in most healthy individuals. However, he remarked that “frequent or excessive consumption can potentially increase the risk of hypertension and cardiac arrhythmias.”.

Industry observers note that an AHA scientific statement published in July 2026 notes that up to 400 milligrams of caffeine daily is generally considered safe for most healthy adults. That’s roughly equivalent to four or five 8-ounce cups of brewed coffee, depending on how it’s prepared.

However, some energy drinks contain up to three times as much caffeine per fluid ounce as brewed coffee.

Certain energy drinks may also contain stimulants, such as guarana, yerba mate, theobromine, synephrine, and yohimbine.

These ingredients may compound caffeine’s effects on the cardiovascular system.

Sources indicate that “Caffeine stimulates the cardiovascular system, primarily by increasing sympathetic nervous system activity. This can cause the heart to beat faster, raise blood pressure, and increase the workload on the heart,” Chen said.

“Energy drinks may contain additional stimulants, such as guarana and taurine, which can further increase blood pressure and stress hormone levels. With excessive consumption, these effects can become more pronounced and potentially interfere with the heart’s normal electrical activity, increasing the risk of abnormal heart rhythms. People with underlying cardiovascular conditions, particularly hypertension or a predisposition to arrhythmias, may be especially vulnerable to these effects.”.

Other research has echoed these concerns. A 2025 review suggests that high-volume energy drink consumption can prolong the heart’s QTc interval, increase blood pressure, and raise heart rate beyond the effects of caffeine alone.

“There is growing concern about the cardiovascular effects of energy drinks and stimulant-containing supplements, particularly among younger adults,” Chen said.

“One challenge is that younger individuals may not recognize that these products can have significant effects on their heart and blood pressure, especially when consumed frequently or in combination with other caffeinated products.”.

Young adults accounted for a substantial portion of the FDA reports included in the study, highlighting potential cardiovascular concerns for this age group.

Recent findings suggest that people with existing heart conditions, a history of irregular heart rhythms, or heightened caffeine sensitivity may face additional risks. Those with undiagnosed genetic heart conditions may also be vulnerable.

A 2024 study identified cases of sudden cardiac arrest occurring shortly after energy drink consumption, particularly among people with underlying inherited heart conditions.

“As a cardiologist, I am particularly concerned about people who may have underlying cardiovascular conditions that have not yet been diagnosed,” Chen said.

Recent findings suggest that “Excessive stimulant intake can potentially trigger symptoms such as palpitations, chest discomfort, and lightheadedness. In susceptible individuals, it may also increase the risk of more serious complications, including abnormal heart rhythms.”.

Additionally, combining energy drinks with strenuous exercise or alcohol may introduce additional cardiovascular risks.

The findings suggest an association between energy drinks, stimulant supplements, and reported cardiovascular events, but they are preliminary and do not establish cause and effect.

The FDA database also relied on voluntary adverse-event reports, meaning some events may never be reported, while others may receive disproportionate attention.

Sources indicate that researchers also do not yet know how many people consumed these products without experiencing any problems. Without this variable, the reports cannot establish actual risk.

Other factors, including underlying health conditions, medications, and lifestyle habits, may also influence the results. More systematic research and controlled clinical trials are needed.

For most healthy adults, consuming up to 400 milligrams of caffeine per day is generally considered safe.

However, Chen noted that individual tolerance for caffeine may vary, and people with underlying cardiovascular conditions, particularly high blood pressure or abnormal heart rhythms, may need to limit or avoid caffeine altogether.

“Energy drinks can vary considerably in their caffeine content and serving sizes,” Chen said.

Recent findings suggest that “Depending on the product, a single can may contain anywhere from 80 to 300 milligrams of caffeine. This means that consuming even one or two energy drinks can put someone close to or above the recommended daily limit, particularly when combined with coffee, tea, or other caffeinated supplements.”.

Seek emergency medical attention if you experience chest pain, particularly if it’s accompanied by shortness of breath, fainting, or other symptoms of a possible heart attack.

If you live with a heart condition, ask your doctor about your daily caffeine intake to determine whether you need to cut back.

According to Chen, warning signs of excessive stimulant intake may include:.

“Depending on the severity of these symptoms, medical attention may be necessary,” he stated.

Recent findings suggest that still, most people may not need to give up caffeine entirely. Monitoring your habits could help protect your heart health. This may include:.

“I encourage people to read product labels carefully and be aware of their total daily caffeine consumption,” Chen said. “I particularly recommend that people with underlying cardiovascular conditions avoid energy drinks.”.

Last But Not Quite Best: Driving the Toyota Supra MkV Final Edition

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1291 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Roadandtrack

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, to this day, the Toyota FT-1 Concept is the most impactful concept car on my psyche.
  • Fast-forward half a decade, and I’m sitting in the driver’s seat of the 2020 Toyota GR Supra 3.0, key in hand, just a year after I started writing about cars for a living.
  • The two-door coupe was spoon-fed minor updates in nearly every year of production, but there were no radical changes along the way.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, to this day, the Toyota FT-1 Concept is the most impactful concept car on my psyche. I remember walking up to it at the Detroit auto show in 2014 and watching it twirl around on the motorized dais for an entirely abnormal amount of time. High school me had no way of knowing it then, but Toyota had plans to make my concept dreams a reality.

Fast-forward half a decade, and I’m sitting in the driver’s seat of the 2020 Toyota GR Supra 3.0, key in hand, just a year after I started writing about cars for a living. The FT-1 Concept to GR Supra transition drew plenty of doubters at the time for its fake vents and very obvious BMW bones, but I hardly cared. Toyota actually built the concept car that I fell so hard for. And now, seven years later, the GR Supra is retiring, with the last of them finally declared gone. Yeah, I’m a little sad.

The two-door coupe was spoon-fed minor updates in nearly every year of production, but there were no radical changes along the way. It’s being put to rest with the most hard-core variant, which Toyota aptly named the MkV Final Edition.

Settling into the driver’s seat, I had hardly any indication of what might be special about this send-off model. Visibility out the letterbox windshield is still atrocious. BMW iDrive 6 (that was never upgraded with Android Auto!) plays on the tacked-on infotainment touchscreen as always. My hand found the shifter directing the BMW-sourced-but-Toyota-improved six-speed manual, and I fired up the turbocharged 3.0-liter inline-six to listen to the same lovely growl.

Industry observers note that before I even pulled out of my neighborhood, the GR team’s efforts to improve handling and stiffen the chassis were evident. This Final Edition is stiff. The list of changes explain the newfound ride deficiencies. Toyota re-tuned the electronically controlled dampers, fitted a stronger front stabilizer bar, installed stiffer bushings in the front control arms, used strengthened rubber mounts for the rear subframe, and added a stronger underbody brace. The Final Edition also runs more aggressive camber in both front and rear, which Toyota says results in greater cornering grip.

Sources indicate that one trip to the grocery store and back was enough for me to determine that this isn’t the Supra you should buy for daily driving duties. Impacts felt way harsher on rough roads, to the level that I questioned whether or not GR went too far in its pursuit of hard-core performance. Meandering around town is clearly not what this car is meant for, so I point it toward the best roads southeast Michigan has to offer.

According to recent reports, as always, the Supra proved to be a rocket when you put the hammer down. The claimed combination of 382 hp and 368 lb-ft of torque still felt like pessimistic numbers given the way the Michelin Pilot Super Sports move. In second, the rear skittered around a bit before the tires hooked up to catapult me forward. The party hardly slowed down as I found third gear, too, the single-turbo inline-six pulling hard all the way to its 6500-rpm redline.

I was a touch put off by the springy clutch-pedal feel, but everything else about this six-speed manual is dynamite. Hitting those two-three then three-two shifts through Michigan’s rolling hills over and over never got old. Toyota did such an excellent job poking and prodding the shifter to improve it over what BMW offered in the Z4 that opting for the manual almost feels like a requirement. Sure, the ZF-sourced eight-speed auto does the job exceptionally well, but the most engaging GR Supras (and the ones that should hold their value the best) will always be the six-speed sticks.

Industry observers note that one of my favorite things about the Supra over the years was just how squirmy and lively it felt under your right foot. This zesty energy is just plain fun when excitement is the priority, but its short wheelbase unpredictability is just as easily a detractor when it comes to pure pace. The Final Edition changes attempt to cure some of this. That strengthened rubber really does bring a greater sense of solidity. The stronger front stabilizer bar and stronger underbody brace in the rear could be felt helping when I rapidly changed direction.

Given a smooth road, the Final Edition felt undoubtedly better put together when I started approaching the limit. It cornered, and more important, transitioned between turns with less hesitation and uncertainty. On a bumpier road, the added stiffness could be a detractor, as the chassis bounces around with a less assuring contact patch. And while Toyota says this special edition has unique differential control tuning, I found the rear was still ready to nip and snap whenever throttle applications grew a little greedy.

Just as in other Supras, driving the Final Edition with pace is an all-immersive experience. I relish a car that makes you work for pace in this way, particularly when it comes to road driving. Sadly, I never drove the Final Edition on the track, but given these upgrades, I suspect it would be the best of the bunch. Toyota claims the larger ducktail carbon-fiber rear spoiler, front wheel-arch flaps, and higher front tire spats all contribute to greater downforce and a better aerodynamic balance at high speeds. Plus, larger Brembo brake discs than the standard car’s should help dissipate heat just a little bit better under higher circuit loadings.

Sources indicate that the experience is a familiar one if you know the Supra well. I absolutely booked it through the straights, egged on by the addictive BMW powerplant, and thoroughly enjoyed the extra confidence of the Final Edition’s stiffening in corners. It’s a shame Toyota never upgraded beyond the Pilot Super Sport tires to the Pilot Sport 4S summer rubber over the years, but I was still able to walk away from my friend tailing me in a new Honda Civic Type R.

In a recent development, stepping out afterward, I’m less than enthused about how Toyota tried to make the Final Edition stand out from an appearance perspective. My test car had the GT4 style pack, which includes an out-of-place “GR” sticker just ahead of the rear wheels. The red mirror caps looked a bit tacky, and the matte black “Supra” badge on the rear could have come straight from Autozone.

It has been revealed that that stated, the Undercover matte-black paint is a nice, exclusive touch if you’re a fan of matte paints. It’s even complemented with 19-inch matte-black wheels to complete the look. No, it’s not my FT-1 dream come to life—I’d need red like the concept car—but I can’t help but admire this car’s curves in its final form.

It has been revealed that is this Final Edition destined to be an all-time great? Sadly, I think not. Rather, it’s best to think of it as one of this fifth-generation’s highlight chapters. It’s technically the most serious and buttoned-down of all the variants, but it also brings some serious compromises on ride and everyday usability to ever-so slightly nudge performance forward. It’s a shame extra power wasn’t on the table.

Industry observers note that as both the Toyota and its BMW Z4 twin leave us, the future of GR seems much brighter than when it arrived. We’ve got a latest Celica on the way! The GR GT is bringing a true flagship experience to the lineup. And while not confirmed, a new Supra feels like an inevitability. I can only hope that these next projects are as teeming with energy and as sonorous as this MkV Supra’s inline-six is.

#224500. Tesla debuts FSD v15, targets its biggest weaknesses, from signs to potholes

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1297 w)
📖 Baca
EV & Auto ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Electrek ↗ Open Full Page

Tesla debuts FSD v15, targets its biggest weaknesses, from signs to potholes

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1297 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Tesla has started rolling out “Full Self-Driving” v15, and its list of improvements reads like a list of FSD’s biggest current weaknesses: sign detection, potholes, and speed handling in school zones.
  • Tesla also claims “25x better handling of safety critical cases” and is adding a new live visualization that looks seriously impressive.
  • Tesla unveiled the rollout on X this afternoon, and its Tesla Super Intelligence account followed up with the full release notes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tesla has started rolling out “Full Self-Driving” v15, and its list of improvements reads like a list of FSD’s biggest current weaknesses: sign detection, potholes, and speed handling in school zones.

Tesla also claims “25x better handling of safety critical cases” and is adding a new live visualization that looks seriously impressive. If the driving improvements are as real as the visuals, this is a big update.

Tesla unveiled the rollout on X this afternoon, and its Tesla Super Intelligence account followed up with the full release notes. The manufacturer didn’t say which vehicles get it first, but it has previously told investors that its AI4 (HW4) computer is enough to run v15.

Here are Tesla’s release notes for FSD v15:.

According to recent reports, v15 upgrades every part of the end-to-end driving network. Includes:.

Sources indicate that tesla’s main announcement also notes FSD can now slow down for speed cameras, and it adds Bike Rack Mode, which allows FSD with a bike rack or a similar hitch accessory. Navigation learning only covers the start and end of trips for now; Tesla says later v15 releases will expand it to the entire route.

Industry observers note that the fresh visualization is the flashiest part, and based on the video Tesla shared, it’s super impressive. The center screen reveals a detailed, rendered version of the street around the car, far beyond the current FSD visualization.

FSD v15 now starting to roll out – upgrading every part of the end-to-end driving network Safety25x better handling of safety critical casesTesla Reality View Adds a live visualization of the drive that lets you see & control what FSD is planning to doNavigation for start… pic.twitter.com/Sfjk4wZecW.

Tesla calls it “Reality View” in its announcement and “Tesla Augmented Reality” in the release notes. The notes say it replaces all the separate model signals with a single end-to-end visualization that uses less compute, and Tesla states it lets the driver “see & control what FSD is planning to do.” If that works as advertised, it could make supervising the system a lot easier.

What stands out more is where Tesla is focusing. Almost every driving improvement in the release notes targets an area where FSD struggles today.

Signs are a massive one. In a test published in September, Brussels nonprofit Johanna.be found that FSD exceeded the limit in 55% of the 30 km/h zones it drove through, averaging 44 km/h. In most of those zones, the car’s screen showed a 50 km/h limit. It didn’t read the sign.

Potholes are another. In August, Musk stated pothole avoidance was “coming soon”, something he had already promised back in 2019. Today, FSD still drives straight through them.

In a recent development, school zones are on the list too. NHTSA is reviewing a petition claiming Tesla’s Robotaxis speed through active school zones, on top of an investigation it opened in October 2025 into FSD traffic-law violations like running red lights. Slowing for speed cameras fits the same theme, though it also suggests Tesla is fine with FSD going over the limit when there’s no camera around.

So if v15 really fixes these, it’s a very good update. The question is by how much.

One change goes the other way. Tesla states it is “decreasing strictness” of driver monitoring in higher-speed driver profiles, at a time when sleeping drivers on FSD keep making headlines and Tesla is tightening monitoring in Europe at regulators’ request.

It has been revealed that the release notes clear up what the “25x” refers to: Tesla indicates the latest vision encoder improves the critical intervention rate by 25x. That’s the right metric to measure progress toward unsupervised driving. But Tesla still doesn’t share the actual number, only the multiplier.

The math gets interesting fast. Our data from earlier this year suggested FSD v14 could go a couple thousand miles between critical interventions. A 25x improvement on that would put v15 around 50,000 miles between critical interventions, well beyond the roughly 10,000 miles we’ve stated Tesla needs for a limited unsupervised service. If that were true across the fleet, we could see Tesla having its most meaningful push toward autonomy in a long time.

Industry observers note that and v15 already carries plenty of hype. In April, Elon Musk wrote that v15 “will far exceed human levels of safety, even in completely unsupervised and complex situations.” We pointed out at the time that he had remarked similar things about v12 and v14. In August, Tesla told JPMorgan that v15 is a “step-change” built on seven “core technologies,” with about 40% of them already running in its Robotaxi fleet in Austin.

FSD has never improved in a straight line. Every major version has brought real gains along with fresh problems, and point releases regularly go backward.

When v14 arrived in October 2025, it came with hallucinations, brake stabbing, and excessive speeding, and early crowdsourced data showed about 732 miles between critical disengagements, below what we expected. It then improved a lot. Then the v14.2 updates went backward before Musk sold v14.3 as the version where “the last major piece of the puzzle finally lands.”.

Seven months and a long string of point releases later, owners are still supervising, and Tesla now needs v15 to deliver what v14.3 was supposed to.

I remain skeptic of Tesla's autonomous driving until they apply for the California DMV permit to begin testing autonomous driving without a driver. California is a big enough of a potential market for robotaxi that Tesla is operating a human driver taxi service. The common presumption is that Tesla is avoiding California autonomous testing because it requires disclosing critical interventions and other data which wouldn't be favorable to Tesla's claims.

Sources indicate that the visuals are super impressive. That much we can already judge from the video, and Reality View could make FSD easier to understand and supervise.

Industry observers note that the driving side is harder to judge. Tesla is going straight at the weaknesses that owners and regulators complain about most: misread speed limits, potholes, school zones, debris. If v15 delivers real progress on all of those, it’s a really good enhancement.

Industry observers note that but “improved detection” doesn’t tell us how much better, and a 25x multiplier without the underlying number is hard to check. FSD has gone two steps forward, one step back throughout its history, with point releases regularly breaking things the previous version handled fine. And Tesla still won’t publish the disengagement data that would settle it.

#224499. What China Taught Me About America's Rambunctious Streak

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (775 w)
📖 Baca
Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Psychologytoday ↗ Open Full Page

What China Taught Me About America's Rambunctious Streak

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (775 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 26, 2026 | Reviewed by Kaja Perina.
  • I've long wondered whether a rambunctious toddler is more likely to develop a balanced temperament than a reticent tike.
  • I bring that up because, having just visited China, I've been thinking about the trajectories of our almost opposite nations.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 26, 2026 | Reviewed by Kaja Perina.

I've long wondered whether a rambunctious toddler is more likely to develop a balanced temperament than a reticent tike. Is a quiet kid more likely to learn boldness than a bold child is to learn when to shut up?

I bring that up because, having just visited China, I've been thinking about the trajectories of our almost opposite nations.

The Chinese are a much more cooperative population than we are. It highlights up even in the fluid dynamics of the society.

According to recent reports, I spent a lot of time walking through non-touristy streets. That's not enough to make me an expert, but I did form impressions. People flow around each other more fluidly than they do here. They're not distracted by each other. They don't nod or look each other in the eye. They simply assume each other. There seems to be no stigma in being glued to a phone.

They're less thirsty for attention. They aren't busy reassuring each other or trying to stand out. They strain less to look and feel exceptional. There were plenty of stylish young people, but not to the extent we see here. Even the ads are less glam.

It has been revealed that it stands to reason. This is a huge, dense urban population whose parents and grandparents, a generation or two ago, were mostly peasants. Their society was shaped by Confucianism 2,500 years ago, a philosophy that is more about etiquette than anything else, at least in its popular form.

Yes, the Chinese have at times gone terribly off the rails. Indonesia also struck me as an extraordinarily tolerant society, yet 60 years ago anti-Communists there slaughtered over a million people. Societies can change. But today China is a mild child. We're the thirsty, intense, fanatical, exceptionalist, rambunctious one.

In a recent development, we distract ourselves with obscene amounts of self-flattery and pandering in commerce and politics. The midterms alone cost 12 billion dollars. All that pandering and flattery doesn't make us wiser. It makes us more anxious and delusional.

According to recent reports, we've just about used up the earth's carrying capacity for self-flattering nonsense. Meanwhile, the demand for flattery and pandering is only getting worse.

In China, there's so little of it, at least so far. That could change, as it did in Indonesia after I visited eight years ago, with the rise of Islamic fundamentalism.

Industry observers note that china doesn't go through the motions of national elections. It's one-party rule, with no pandering and a focus on practical welfare that, on my visit, went far beyond what we see here. They proposal to double their train lines by 2035. There's practically no theft in the city center, and the cameras are everywhere, so you'd get caught and punished. China's Gini coefficient, a measure of wealth inequality, is around 35. Ours is about ten points higher.

On my two trips there, I met only one Christian. It's an atheist country, and you can't talk about the supernatural as real. There's none of our jersey-wearing, lifestyle-brand supernaturalist grandstanding and infighting.

In a recent development, people grumble about the lack of freedom of speech, but they can grumble without looking over their shoulders. At Peking University, built on the land of the emperor's Summer Palace and just a few blocks from the government center, a professor told me that, paradoxically, they have more freedom of speech there. In distant cities, you have to attend a Communist Party meeting every two weeks. At the university, you just fill out minutes. There are limits, though. You can't talk casually about Mao on social media, and you can't call him a dictator. They're trying to put the violence of the 1966-76 Cultural Revolution behind them, along with the poverty. In 1976, China's average income was a third of Sub-Saharan Africa's. They've come a long way. Maybe they'll keep going.

Recent findings suggest that if you're not watching China, you should be. Odds are they will surpass us, and Pax Americana will give way to Pax Sinica. Since I study American fanaticism, I could get a distorted view of humankind. China makes me think humankind might pull off some kind of harmony. It fills me with optimism about human potential.

And maybe we'll learn from China's success. Maybe the rambunctious child will learn to chill out. We had better.

Maybe we'll converge on some mix of reticent and rambunctious that makes humankind survivable.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that the latest HoYoverse Special Program has brought us big Genshin Impact news. Version Luna 3 has been fully revealed, continuing the Nod-Krai story. The upcoming chapter arrives December 3 across all platforms.

The Moon-Prayer Night is the major in-world festival, marking Dameselette's final night before she sets off for the moon. The latest revision, of course, introduces new playable characters, one with an interesting mechanic.

Sources indicate that the events of this fresh chapter take place following Rarcher of Solnari’s defeat. The victory has given way to the Moon-Prayer Night celebrations, which brings various stalls to the Nasha Town, alongside a new souvenir stamp book where you can record your memories.

All is not fine, however, as Alice and Nicole Reeyn come bearing some bad news about phantoms appearing across the Nod-Krai region at Teyvat's borders. There’s a mystery to be uncovered here, and your journey to do so won’t be a lonely one.

Industry observers note that the highly-anticipated Durin is at last the upcoming playable character. A 5-Star Pyro Sword wielder, Durin can switch between two different forms: one lets him deal damage, while the other is best suited to supporting the team.

Industry observers note that durin was once a dragon, you see, who was later given a human body. This is why he’s able to switch forms. The more powerful, Abyssal-infused form can launch major attacks on single targets to boost his own Vaporize and Melt damage, while his support form reduces enemies’ Elemental Resistance and deals AoE Pyro damage.

Durin’s Story Quest will shed more light on that aspect of his life, and completing it earns you a reward for him. Speaking of quests, completing the Archon Quest will grant you 500 Primogems. As a member of Hexenzirkel, Durin and other characters can gain new powers when you complete more quests in Moon-Prayer Night.

All characters connected to the Hexenzirkel can benefit from certain story quests tied to their abilities. This is a big new addition, and will affect Venti, Klee, Albedo, Mona, Razor, Fischl, and Sucrose - all of whom can become Hexerei characters. This ties into the new Hexerei Secret Rite effect, which will trigger when two or more Hexerei characters are present. The effect boosts the entire party’s combat effectiveness.

Sources indicate that the other new character in Luna 3 is Jahoda, a 4-Star Anemo Bow wielder who’s great at healing teammates and absorbing Elements, which she can then use to deal damage. The first phase of Luna 3 will feature Durin and Jahoda, alongside the return of Venti. The second phase sees no new character debuts, but does feature the return of Varesa and Xilonen.

Sources indicate that there’s more to get excited about in Luna 3, even if you don’t feel like spending most of your time in Nod-Krai. The Soulblazers' Snowbound Journey event will take you back to Dragonspine, where you’ll find winter-theme minigames appropriate to an revision cycle spanning December to January. This is how you can earn the 4-Star Rainbow Serpent's Rain Bow, too.

Beyond that, you can also look forward to the Miliastra Wonderland UGC module getting newly introduced updates. The Wonderland Resource Center is where creators can get and share resources through the editing tool.

New Food Pyramid Puts Healthy Carbs and Plant-Based Foods First

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A first-of-its-kind international food pyramid, developed by 22 leading nutritionists from Europe, Canada, the United States, and Australia, was published in Advances in Nutrition in September.
  • This new food pyramid emphasizes plant-based protein sources, cooking with plant-based oils, and healthier sugars and carbohydrates.
  • It also echoes the traditional food pyramid used in the United States since 1992.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A first-of-its-kind international food pyramid, developed by 22 leading nutritionists from Europe, Canada, the United States, and Australia, was published in Advances in Nutrition in September.

This new food pyramid emphasizes plant-based protein sources, cooking with plant-based oils, and healthier sugars and carbohydrates.

It also echoes the traditional food pyramid used in the United States since 1992.

The latest pyramid breaks away from the Trump administration’s updated nutritional guidelines, which are part of Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s Make America Health Again (MAHA) agenda and prioritize red meat over plants.

Industry observers note that the latest pyramid was designed by a research team led by Brigham Young University professor Karen Della Corte. The researchers noted that this is the first international food pyramid that is designed to reflect scientific agreement across multiple countries and cultures.

Della Corte and researchers from the International Carbohydrate Quality Consortium (ICQC), compared dietary guidelines from multiple countries, including:.

They also analyzed evidence from more than 250 scientific publications, while drawing on the EAT-Lancet Planetary Health Diet to identify principles of healthy eating that may be shared.

The upcoming pyramid highlights three guidelines:.

While the pyramid emphasizes plant-based proteins, it doesn’t exclude animal proteins.

“I find the new international food pyramid a more practical and aligned approach for the prevention of chronic disease,” said Michelle Routhenstein, Preventive Cardiology Dietitian at Entirely Nourished, who wasn’t involved in the creation of the food pyramid.

“The upcoming international food pyramid places greater emphasis on food quality and the importance of building meals around nutrient-dense plant foods, while still allowing room for lean animal proteins such as fish, poultry, eggs, and yogurt,” she added.

Sources indicate that while the new pyramid and the current U.S. dietary guidelines differ in many ways, they also agree on certain factors.

For example, both sets of guidelines discourage added sugars, refined carbs, and highly processed snacks.

Industry observers note that the differences between the two mainly lie in their emphasis on specific sources of protein and fat. For example, the fresh pyramid prioritizes plant-based proteins, while the U.S. guidelines place greater emphasis on animal proteins, including red meat.

While both sets of recommendations advise limiting saturated fat, the upcoming pyramid emphasizes unsaturated plant oils, whereas the U.S. guidelines also include butter and beef tallow as cooking fat options.

Routhenstein noted that an crucial distinction is that this new pyramid goes beyond simply telling people to eat more protein or fewer carbohydrates. Instead, it encourages people to consider the quality and sources of those nutrients.

However, the main emphasis of both guidelines is encouraging people to eat fewer ultra-processed foods and more natural or “real” foods.

Routhenstein told Healthline that research consistently shows that plant-forward eating patterns, including the Mediterranean and DASH diets, are associated with better cardiovascular health and a lower risk of heart disease.

Plant foods provide fiber, potassium, antioxidants, and other beneficial compounds that can help support healthy cholesterol levels, blood pressure, blood sugar, and blood vessel function.

“This is not to say that protein and fat are unimportant, but their sources matter,” Routhenstein said.

In a statement from BYU, Della Corte shared the following tips for incorporating the fresh pyramid’s recommendations into your diet:.

Industry observers note that the pyramid is a framework, not a personalized prescription. If you have questions about your individual nutritional needs, you can speak with your healthcare professional or a licensed dietitian.

“It is important to recognize that plant-forward does not mean vegan or vegetarian. The amount and sources of animal protein should be considered to ensure they align with an individual’s cardiometabolic goals and lab targets,” Routhenstein stated.

💡 Key Takeaways
