Plant-Based Milk Alternatives May Not Give You Enough Iodine. Here’s Why That Matters

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (717 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Healthline

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Replacing dairy with plant-based alternatives (PBAs), even partially, could substantially lower iodine intake, especially if those alternatives aren’t fortified, according to a recent study published in the Lancet Planetary Health.
  • The United Kingdom-based researchers found that only 12% of UK plant-based milk, yogurt, and cheese products analyzed were fortified with iodine.
  • In the United States, the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) provides guidance on the nutritional content of PBAs, but fortification with iodine is voluntary.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Replacing dairy with plant-based alternatives (PBAs), even partially, could substantially lower iodine intake, especially if those alternatives aren’t fortified, according to a recent study published in the Lancet Planetary Health.

The United Kingdom-based researchers found that only 12% of UK plant-based milk, yogurt, and cheese products analyzed were fortified with iodine. This compares with 61% for calcium and 46% for vitamin B12.

In the United States, the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) provides guidance on the nutritional content of PBAs, but fortification with iodine is voluntary.

The study found that replacing as little as 20% of dairy intake with plant-based alternatives could increase the risk of inadequate iodine intake, particularly among adolescent girls and women of reproductive age.

“People often worry about a decline in calcium intake when they replace some of their dairy with plant-based alternatives. As a result, iodine is frequently overlooked. This study serves as a valuable reminder of iodine’s significance as a nutrient,” said Victoria Finn, MD, board certified endocrinologist at Medical Offices of Manhattan, who wasn’t involved in the study.

The study included analysis of UK plant-based milk, cheese, and yogurt products, as well as dietary data from 3,500 people.

The researchers used statistical modeling to predict how swapping dairy for PBAs might affect iodine and other nutrients.

The people who are most vulnerable to iodine inadequacy are adolescent females and people at reproductive age, especially those who are pregnant or who strategy to become pregnant.

The researchers estimated that replacing 20% to 35% of dairy intake with PBAs would increase the proportion of people with inadequate iodine intake:.

In a recent development, when the researchers modeled the replacement of all dairy products with PBAs, the proportion of adolescent females with inadequate iodine intake rose to 80%. Among females ages 19 to 49, that proportion remained relatively stable as replacement rates increased.

It is important to keep in mind that the study used dietary modeling rather than direct measurement of iodine status.

Iodine is key for thyroid hormone production, metabolism, and both fetal and child brain development.

“Your thyroid gland requires iodine to produce thyroid hormones, which play a crucial role in regulating metabolism and supporting normal growth and development,” remarked Finn.

According to recent reports, she added that if you consistently consume too little iodine over an extended period, the thyroid gland may enlarge and eventually struggle to produce enough hormones. This condition is known as hypothyroidism, which can lead to various symptoms such as lethargy, sleepiness, weight gain, dry skin, and more.

“Hypothyroidism can be particularly dangerous during pregnancy, as the baby’s brain, nervous system, and organs rely heavily on the mother’s thyroid hormone during the early stages of development,” Finn added.

In the United Kingdom, dairy is a major iodine source due to cattle feed supplementation, not because dairy is naturally high in iodine.

In the United States, dairy is also an vital source of iodine for the same reasons.

However, the risk profile for iodine deficiency in the U.S. may differ from the U.K., as iodized salt is also a significant source of iodine and is widely available in the U.S., but not in the U.K.

According to the National Institutes of Health (NIH), the recommended daily intake of iodine depends on your age.

Plant-based or plant-forward diets have grown in popularity, in part due to the health benefits they offer. For example, consuming less meat can reduce your risk of heart disease, type 2 diabetes, obesity, and high cholesterol.

Sources indicate that however, as this study suggests, it may be possible to reduce your iodine intake when transitioning to a plant-based diet. There are ways you can protect your iodine intake when choosing a more plant-forward diet, though.

It has been revealed that check the labels on plant-based dairy alternatives to find those fortified with iodine. You can also read the nutrition label. Iodine may be listed as potassium iodide or potassium iodate.

Seafood, eggs, and iodized salt are all good sources of iodine.

You can also discuss iodine supplements with your healthcare professional.

Industry observers note that “Iodine supplements should be taken with caution, especially without checking your thyroid levels,” said Finn. “Additionally, be cautious with kelp supplements, as their iodine content can vary, and excessive iodine intake can disrupt thyroid function.”.

‘Vibe coding’ is risky: Here’s why and what to do about it

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Thanks to rapid advances in AI chatbots like ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude, “vibe coding” is very much a possibility for anyone: Just use natural language to explain what you want a program to do, and the AI will put it together for you.
  • This has led non-programmers to swiftly create their own sites and apps, and you’ll find a multitude of examples online.
  • According to recent reports, vibe-coding gadgets can lead to some impressive demonstrations of AI’s current capabilities, but is it wise to try it at home on the devices you use every day?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Thanks to rapid advances in AI chatbots like ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude, “vibe coding” is very much a possibility for anyone: Just use natural language to explain what you want a program to do, and the AI will put it together for you.

This has led non-programmers to swiftly create their own sites and apps, and you’ll find a multitude of examples online. Vibe coding has extended to hardware too—whether it’s people hacking into their 1994 Cherokee Jeep or repurposing an Amazon Kindle.

According to recent reports, vibe-coding gadgets can lead to some impressive demonstrations of AI’s current capabilities, but is it wise to try it at home on the devices you use every day? Probably not, and we’ll explain why here.

If you’ve never used an AI app to vibe code—or used an AI app at all—then you might be wondering what all the talk about vibe coding actually means. It’s the widely used, informal term for prompting an AI chatbot to create a program: Maybe you want a phone app to track your exercise, for example, or a simple game you can play in your browser.

According to recent reports, as long as your ambitions aren’t too grand—you’re not going to get GTA VI out of this anytime soon—your AI engine of choice will produce a slick, usable, custom-made app for you within a few minutes. If there are any bugs or problems (and there often are), then you can use follow-up prompts to get rid of them.

While the end results might need a bit of finessing and don’t match up to what a team of professional software developers can do, it’s incredible to think that AI now enables anyone to write apps of their own, no manual coding required. Need a registration website for your sports club or an app to track trains at your local station? Just ask for it.

It has been revealed that that’s not to say there aren’t downsides to vibe coding, though, which we’ll get to next. AI code isn’t always the most reliable or efficient, and you need to be aware of its limitations—and put safeguards in place to make sure there’s no danger of vibe-coded apps causing issues for other hardware and software.

Sources indicate that as TechCrunch reports, television sets are common targets for some vibe-coded tinkering. Consumers are using code produced by AI apps to simplify the app launchers, take out sponsored content and advertising, and turn off some of the aggressive tracking features that come with modern-day TVs, for example.

Here’s the problem: While the AI app developers don’t often mention it, AI code often comes with bugs and unintended consequences attached, and if you don’t understand what you’re coding, then you can’t fix it. That’s not so much of an glitch if you’re trying to get a custom soccer score tracker running in your browser, but if you’re suddenly bricking your main TV, then that is a problem.

The operating systems on TVs—as well as tablets, laptops, speakers, fridges, and other gadgets—can be complex, and AIs will often guess at what the right approach is if they don’t know for sure. You risk breaking key functionality, creating upcoming bugs while trying to fix existing ones, and leaving security vulnerabilities open that hackers can target.

Of course it’s easy to see the appeal of an ad-free TV that runs faster than before, but is it worth opening up your television set to malware? Or not being able to use the Netflix app for reasons you can’t fathom? Or one day finding that it’s stuck in an endless loop between shutting down and powering up? These are the risks of vibe coding.

Sources indicate that different categories of devices work in different ways, but you’ll often find that there are more reliable ways of customizing your hardware than relying on something you’ve vibe-coded yourself. When it comes to TVs, for example, there are often alternative launchers available, such as Projectivy Launcher for Google TV models, which is ad-free and offers a ton of customization options.

For routers, there’s something like OpenWrt, which is built and maintained by a large enthusiast community. It lets you do all sorts of things with compatible routers, including blocking ads and trackers, customizing which devices can access the network and when, monitoring bandwidth, and integrating a VPN at the router level.

If you’re looking to do more with your smart home devices, then Home Assistant is definitely worth a look. The popular alternative smart home system management software gives you much more control over your devices and what you can do with them than the comparable apps offered by Amazon, Google, and Apple.

You’re still putting your faith in third-party code that you haven’t personally written—but these projects are managed by capable software developers and backed by big user communities that monitor complications like security and compatibility. When it comes to keeping your gadgets usable, they’re the safer bet.

#224466. Why Couldn’t I Be Happy for Someone I Love?

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (891 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Psychologytoday ↗ Open Full Page

Why Couldn’t I Be Happy for Someone I Love?

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (891 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 26, 2026 | Reviewed by Kaja Perina.
  • This article was written in collaboration with Anna Goldfarb, author of Modern Friendship.
  • With the holidays upon us, many of us will gather with loved ones, sharing platefuls of food, laughter, and important updates about our lives.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 26, 2026 | Reviewed by Kaja Perina.

This article was written in collaboration with Anna Goldfarb, author of Modern Friendship.

With the holidays upon us, many of us will gather with loved ones, sharing platefuls of food, laughter, and important updates about our lives. If you’re recently engaged, expecting, or have received an impressive accolade at work, what better time to announce the news than when you’re all in the same room?

But hearing someone’s good news can be unexpectedly fraught, especially if you’re struggling. You might want to rejoice for them but find you can’t. By understanding why good news is uniquely powerful in making or breaking a relationship, you can navigate the holidays with self-compassion and avoid a sting from swelling into something bigger.

In a recent development, when we receive a friend’s bad news, we learn where we stand in their life. Finding out about our friend’s surgery through the grapevine, for example, reveals something about the closeness of the bond: the earlier we’re told, the closer we feel to that friend.

Sources indicate that if you find out you’re not in their inner circle of confidantes, it can make you question how close your friendship even was: “Fluffy died, and you didn’t tell me? Am I even your best friend?”.

Good news reveals closeness too. Researchers call it a norm of close friendship to share good news, so when we don’t, our friends may question how close we are. When we hide good news from others, research finds, they report feeling more insulted and less close to us.

Recent findings suggest that hearing that a dear friend is engaged, expecting, or has scored a promotion reshapes how we think about our own experience. While we may have felt at peace with our job title, hearing that a friend got promoted may make us suddenly feel inadequate. We compare our friend’s newly achieved status to our own, and make inferences regarding our value. Good news, then, forces us to confront our status.

Industry observers note that of course, this doesn’t happen all the time. If someone else’s positive news is in an area you don’t identify with, you can revel in their success. Your friend can win an award for being the best baker in the tri-state area. If you don’t care about being an elite baker, cheering them on doesn’t require you to measure yourself against them. However, if you also dream of being an accomplished baker, it will be much harder to be happy for them because of what their good news means for you.

Abraham Tesser’s Self-Evaluation Maintenance Model (1988) explains this well. His model predicts that when someone close to you outperforms you in an area central to who you are and what you care about, the comparison uniquely stings. That’s why we might take someone’s good news personally.

Here are two questions to help you figure out why you couldn’t be happy for someone when you wanted to be:.

Answers to the first question are usually:.

Each feeling points to a source.

Answers to the second question can reveal common closeness and status concerns:.

I wasn’t told when I expected to be.

I felt unimportant to my friend.

I wasn’t sure what it meant for me moving forward.

I felt less content with my own life.

Sources indicate that sometimes the answer is simpler: I wanted it for myself. That’s envy, and it’s normal.

Industry observers note that as you hear happy updates from others this holiday season, be gentle with yourself, as you might’ve just learned something new about your relationship with the other person. It’s normal to have complicated feelings in the moment.

If you felt excluded because you weren’t told when you expected to be, start by celebrating their news, if you can. Later, you can let them know you’d love to hear updates sooner: “I love hearing your news. I hope you know you can always come to me with things like this.” Opening the conversation this way will hopefully give you more insight into their thinking. It also helps to reflect on who heard first and why. Do those people play a bigger role in your friend’s life right now? Are there sensible reasons your friend told other people first? Perhaps this friend shares work updates with you, but keeps personal updates to another circle. Now you know how they regard your relationship, and you can recalibrate your expectations.

Industry observers note that if you felt inadequate after hearing the news, you’ll probably need some time and space to process the jolt. For example, if your friend is having a baby and you’ve recently had a miscarriage, you can tell your friend, “I’m so happy for you, and I need a little time to take it in. I’ll call you this weekend.” If you simply wanted the thing for yourself, own it: I wanted that job. Envy points to something you want, and you can still show up warmly while the envious feeling settles.

By understanding why you’re struggling to be happy for people you love, you give yourself the best chance of keeping the relationship once the feelings pass.

#224465. The best way to pack a suitcase, according to science

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1501 w)

The best way to pack a suitcase, according to science

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1501 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that while recently packing for an overseas excursion, I stuffed every spare space I could find in my carry-on.
  • Industry observers note that to find out how best to pack according to science, Popular Science turned to Anne McAlpin, a travel expert and author of the book, Pack it Up: the Essential Guide to Smart Travel.
  • Many carry-on bags have “ruts” or internal grooves to accommodate a recessed trolley handle.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that while recently packing for an overseas excursion, I stuffed every spare space I could find in my carry-on. I used what I call the “Mary Poppins” packing method: willing myself to believe that whatever I wanted to put in my luggage would fit, regardless of the size of the object or the size of my bag. Somehow my system worked, but when I arrived at my destination and unzipped my bag, everything within it exploded onto the floor. “There’s gotta be a better way,” I thought.

Industry observers note that to find out how best to pack according to science, Popular Science turned to Anne McAlpin, a travel expert and author of the book, Pack it Up: the Essential Guide to Smart Travel. Over the course of her lifetime, McAlpin has estimated she’s packed—and unpacked—more than 25,000 times! She’s a whiz at minimizing dead space, maximizing volume, and keeping clothes looking more like they came off a closet hanger than straight out of a laundry bin.

Many carry-on bags have “ruts” or internal grooves to accommodate a recessed trolley handle. This handle uses two narrow metal poles that retract straight into the middle or sides of the interior lining, causing the interior surface of the suitcase to be uneven.

Industry observers note that “If you don’t have a flat foundation, make one,” says McAlpin. Having a flat foundation maximizes space, prevents wrinkles, and adds stability to your bag. To do this, consider evening out the space between ruts with packing or compression cubes. “You can put all of your underwear into a compression cube,” a small bag made of breathable nylon or polyester mesh used in part to organize items, and then place it between the ruts. This will even out the bottom of a hard-shell suitcase. Flexible items such as toiletry kits and rolled-up socks can help to form this base layer as well. “I then pack my clothing on top of that flat foundation.”.

In a recent development, mcAlpin puts her shoes (she usually packs two pairs and wears a third) towards the bottom of the suitcase so that the weight is on the wheels. “You don’t want to put your heavy items on the top of the inside of your suitcase,” she states. “This will cause it to constantly topple.”.

When it comes to clothing, McAlpin rolls some items and flat packs others. “I call it interlayering,” she says.

For example, with pants, rather than folding them to stack in a pile, McAlpin lays each pair out along its natural creases as if she were going to put them on a hanger. Then, she places them in her suitcase: waistband at the top of one side of the bag, legs dangling out the other side of the bag. They’re not folded, but laid out straight. This way, McAlpin can then wrap them around the rolled items that she’ll later place on top of them.

She does the same with cotton shirts, sundresses—anything that might wrinkle. With each item, McAlpin alternates the direction, so that there are no two waistbands or shirt collars bulking up one side of the suitcase.

“I then roll my knit items and synthetic things that don’t wrinkle as much. I roll them up like Tootsie Rolls and I place them side by side,” in the middle of the laid-out items. While folding clothes and stacking them leaves pockets of air both inside the folds and within the layers, rolling wraps fabrics into a smooth, tight cylinder, which reduces the overall amount of space each item uses. It’s the best of both worlds! Your laid-out items aren’t as wrinkled and your wrinkle-resistant items are more tightly packed. This allows for more room in your suitcase overall.

Industry observers note that when McAlpin has all her rolled items tightly packed together, she takes the pant legs and skirts that are still hanging off the sides of the suitcase, and “bends them up and over the ‘roll bar’ I’ve made of sweaters, pajamas, and sweats.” This helps avoid the knee creases that come when you’re simply folding pants. It also keeps items compact, and is a game-changer when it comes to unpacking. You can just lift all of the interlayered items out of your suitcase in one fell swoop.

Fill up empty space. For example, McAlpin says that if you’re a couple packing together, you may be able to slide a woman’s sandal right into a man’s shoe, or at least use the shoe’s interior cavity to store phone chargers, socks, or small items like earrings and even an eyeglasses case. Not only is it a space-saver, but filling up unused space prevents transit damage by keeping items inside from shifting.

In a recent development, stuff the corners of a suitcase with socks, rolled-up t-shirts, etc, “because all those awkward corners offer prime packing space,” notes McAlpin. Filling up those pockets also distributes structural stress throughout the bag, helping to keep features like zippers and fabric intact during excessive handling.

Industry observers note that is turbulence really like Jell-O? Pilots weigh in.

In a recent development, why do our ears pop on a plane? An audiologist explains.

According to recent reports, why do we put seatbacks up for landing? An aviation expert explains.

Another trick: laying belts around the luggage perimeter so that they’re easier to find.

According to recent reports, to keep things condensed and organized, McAlpin suggests compression cubes. These small bags feature two zippers: a main zipper that closes the cube like a standard bag, and a second perimeter zipper that pulls the cube’s top and bottom panels closer together, squeezing out excess air and reducing volume. Compression cubes help eliminate air pockets that come with traditional folding and can reduce the volume of soft clothes like T-shirts and pants up to 30 percent.

Another option: roll-up compression bags. These pump-free, vacuum-free storage bags use one-way pressure valves to push air out, cutting volume by up to 80 percent. “I use these for laundry,” claims McAlpin, because they temporarily block odors.

“They’re like an industrial Ziploc bag,” she says, and great for bulky items like a fleece jacket. But use them sparingly. Roll sacks are typically made of plastic and cause a lot more wrinkles than traditional compression cubes.

Industry observers note that mcAlpin carries dry laundry sheets and a two-gallon Ziploc bag for washing clothes. “The bag doesn’t take up any room, and then I can wash my socks and underwear without worrying if I’ve left any toothpaste in the sink.”.

McAlpin indicates her packing “3:1 ratio” (three tops to every bottom) has “changed people’s lives.” She packs nine tops and three bottoms, and everything mixes and matches. “I base everything around two colors,” she says, “like a black and a tan,” and then throws in an occasional splash of color.

Recent findings suggest that this works, claims McAlpin, because human memory registers outfits based on what’s closest to the head and face. And while she travels with three pairs of shoes, each one should be for something different. For example, runners for long walks, sandals for the beach, and loafers for evenings.

Recent findings suggest that as for the bag itself, McAlpin indicates four-wheel bags (spinner luggage) are a must. Not only are they easy to maneuver through packed terminals and airplane aisles, the ability to push the bag upright beside you keeps your arm in a neutral, bent-elbow position. This places less stress on your wrists, shoulders, and lower back compared to pulling a two-wheel bag behind you, and plays a big role in easing ergonomic strain.

It has been revealed that they’re also ideal for stacking, since they stay upright. Think about it, claims McAlpin. “When you pack your heavy tote bag on top of your suitcase, it’s the bag, not your shoulders, that’s carrying the weight.”.

Ultimately, the idea is to make use of all your space, keep items from bumping around inside your suitcase and (if possible) wrinkle-free, and to not throw out your back in the process.

Of course, when it comes to finding room for souvenirs, there’s always the Mary Poppins packing method. But after talking with McAlpin, I’ve been using her method exclusively. My clothes, formerly creased, rumpled, and crinkled, are now decidedly wrinkle-free!

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Battlefield Studios is seemingly trying something different with Battlefield 6’s next patch, which everyone assumed would be a standard, mid-season update not intended to change the game significantly.

However, it appears that it may bring more to the game than we realised, enough that the developer sees it as an excuse to bring back the pre-launch Battlefield Labs testing initiative.

Industry observers note that the December 9 patch kicks off the final phase of the game’s first season, which is set to take the game through the holidays and into the new year. We’ve known about its content for a while, and it’s definitely the lightest, compared to the two previous phases.

Battlefield Studios confirmed a host of upcoming changes that will be included in the same patch, which are apparently significant enough to require player testing. The developer is reviving Battlefield Labs to help it do so, but only for three two-hour sessions, split across the game’s three main server regions (EU, NA, APAC).

Recent findings suggest that all tests are scheduled for today, December 2, and they remain under NDA. Battlefield Labs is also sticking with PC as its chosen platform yet again, though you will be able to join through Steam this time, alongside the EA app.

In a recent development, the focus of the test will be on three key areas that the December 9 patch will be touching. First, there’s footstep audio, an glitch that was really brought into focus with the launch of Redsec Battle Royale. You can expect to hear enemy footsteps from farther away, and intuitively know the type of surface they’re moving on.

Industry observers note that the patch also brings another pass to hit registration and netcode, which BF Studios says should improve responsiveness in close-quarter situations. Finally, there are broader changes to other combat areas that the announcement didn’t elaborate on.

All testing will take place on Eastwood, and Operation Firestorm, rotating between Conquest, and Escalation.

Industry observers note that going forward, Battlefield Studios said to expect Labs to be open to more players, and for the process itself to be smoother. The developer wants to have faster turnaround times, after all, so that the initiative can test smaller changes and be more responsive to player feedback.

Some of the more involved, future sessions will include experiments with map layout changes and various other non-standard compositions of player and vehicle numbers. Of course, you can also expect new maps and modes to be tested in Labs, similar to how the CTE was used in Battlefield 4’s long life.

How a red wolf gets a checkup

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (374 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that annual human checkups are relatively straightforward.
  • It has been revealed that we’ve previously discovered that conducting a checkup on a 140 pound stingray takes eight people, that you can weigh an octopus with a laundry basket, and that bears should always be under anesthesia before their exam.
  • “The biggest difference is the level of restraint or sedation needed for red wolves, since they are wild animals and not habituated to human contact,” she tells Popular Science.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that annual human checkups are relatively straightforward. You hop onto the exam table, stick your tongue out, stare straight ahead as the doctor beams light into your eyes, let them tap their small hammer against that wildly uncomfortable spot under your kneecap, etc. But for wildlife, it’s a whole other experience.

It has been revealed that we’ve previously discovered that conducting a checkup on a 140 pound stingray takes eight people, that you can weigh an octopus with a laundry basket, and that bears should always be under anesthesia before their exam. But what about another favorite carnivore—wolves? According to Vicki Scharfberg, from Roger Williams Park Zoo & Carousel Village in Rhode Island, the annual wellness examination for red wolves (Canis rufus) is not that different from a pet dog’s annual veterinary visit.

“The biggest difference is the level of restraint or sedation needed for red wolves, since they are wild animals and not habituated to human contact,” she tells Popular Science.

The checkup includes a physical examination at the wolf enclosure or the zoo veterinary hospital, bloodwork, vaccinations, heartworm prevention care, and if necessary, parasite treatment. A social media post by Roger Williams Park Zoo showcases their red wolf named Frye thoroughly knocked out on the exam table, undergoing an oral exam, among other things.

Sources indicate that the team uses the bloodwork to check on the wolf’s organs and screen for heartworm disease. Interestingly, their vaccines are the exact same ones veterinarians give to domestic dogs for rabies, distemper, parvovirus, and leptospirosis.

Sources indicate that heartworm prevention treatment involves a long-acting 12 month injection. Heartworm disease is caused by grossly long worms called heartworms that take up residence in an animals’ heart, lungs, and related blood vessels. This parasitic condition triggers severe lung disease, heart failure, and damages other organs. Heartworm is potentially fatal, and in addition to wolves can also impact animals including dogs, cats, ferrets, foxes, and humans.

“If something abnormal is found on the examination, we follow up with additional diagnostics like x-rays, ultrasound, or a consult with a veterinary specialist (dentist, cardiologist, etc),” Scharfberg concludes.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • In the same vein as its predecessor, the 296 Challenge Stradale is a road car that shares its fundamental philosophy with the upcoming 296 Challenge Evo racecar, which will debut in the single-marque Ferrari Challenge racing series next year.
  • See all results for Ferrari 296 for sale near 07011.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Nostalgia must be in the air in Maranello. A few months ago, Ferrari unveiled the 12Cilindri Manuale, reintroducing a (simulated) six-speed manual transmission to its model lineup purely for the sake of driver involvement. And now, the Challenge Stradale badge returns to the rear engine mesh of a Prancing Horse for the first time since the 360 CS was discontinued in 2004. Simply put, it's a good year to be a sentimental Ferrarista.

In the same vein as its predecessor, the 296 Challenge Stradale is a road car that shares its fundamental philosophy with the upcoming 296 Challenge Evo racecar, which will debut in the single-marque Ferrari Challenge racing series next year. Parked side by side at their reveal at the Circuit de Barcelona-Catalunya today, we would excuse a gentleman driver for confusing the CS with his new track-only machinery.

See all results for Ferrari 296 for sale near 07011.

There have been several limited-edition, track-focused mid-engine Ferraris since the 360 Challenge Stradale—including the F430 Scuderia, 458 Speciale, and 488 Pista—but the 296 Challenge Stradale goes the furthest of all of them in emulating its racecar counterpart, both aesthetically and mechanically.

While previous track-centric Ferraris have been somewhat demurely styled, the 296 CS puts its aerodynamic elements on full display. The carbon-fiber rear wing, dive planes, adjustable front splitter, and vented hood are essentially a copy-paste job from the Challenge Evo, with concessions made for road legality. Up front, twin vents positioned in the hood just before the windshield channel hot air expelled from two under-hood radiators over the windshield and towards the rear of the car, reducing the aerodynamic variations caused by changing ground clearance.

Other aero features are hidden out of sight. The CS's underbody has been smoothed to better feed the rear diffuser and work with three pairs of vortex generators at the front and two at the rear to generate additional downforce. With all of the aerodynamic elements colluding, the 296 Challenge Stradale makes 1360 pounds of downforce at 155 mph. That's a 72-percent increase over the base 296GTB's peak figure.

In a recent development, major changes have been made to the CS's powertrain. You won't find any orange high-voltage wiring snaking around under the glass of its mid-mounted hood like you would in a 296GTB or 296 Speciale, as the 5-kWh battery pack and rear-mounted axial-flux electric motor have been removed entirely. The twin-turbo 3.0-liter V-6 operates unassisted and supposedly sounds better than ever courtesy of a reworked twin-exit exhaust system.

See all results for Ferrari 296 for sale near 07011.

In a recent development, overall firepower has decreased to 670 horsepower—149 ponies less than the standard 296GTB's. The upside is a notable decrease in mass, with Ferrari claiming that the removal of the plug-in-hybrid componentry played a major role in shedding 328 pounds from the 296GTB's dry weight. A lightened transmission flex plate, driveshaft, and timing cover were also developed to make the CS's powertrain as featherweight as possible. Without an electric motor present to fill in any thrust gaps left by turbo lag, the V-6 has been retuned to increase low-end grunt, although peak torque remains 546 pound-feet delivered at 6250 rpm.

Recent findings suggest that as to be expected, yanking out an integrated powertrain system comes with some unique challenges that affect more than just the engine itself. For example, Ferrari was forced to enlarge the 296 CS's rear carbon-ceramic brake rotors and the ventilation ducts that cool them to compensate for the lack of regenerative braking. The decreased weight in the rear also shifted its weight distribution 1.5 percent to the front, which was addressed with suspension design and geometry changes.

The CS's newly developed suspension is derived directly from the 296 Challenge Evo and features semi-active dampers and a dual-spring design that improves rebound response. The result is reduced body roll, which helps the performance of the specially developed Pirelli P Zero R and P Zero Trofeo RS tires, measuring 245/35ZR-20 in the front and 305/35ZR-20 in the rear. The 20-inch forged wheels can be ordered in Matte Grigio Corsa, Matte Nero with a diamond-cut finish, or Matte Bianco Fuji.

The 296 Challenge Stradale's cockpit is very similar to the one found in the 296 Speciale. While niceties like climate control and a stereo remain, carbon-fiber door panels and a lack of armrests and storage pockets are a clear indication of the CS's weight-saving mission. For true gluttons for punishment, an even further stripped interior spec is available that removes the trim from the area beneath the seats and the lower section of the carpets beneath the center console, leaving part of the chassis exposed.

Ferrari is adamant that the 296 CS isn't a replacement for the 296 Speciale and will not cannibalize that model's customer base, as the two are intended for different buyers. Besides being geared less towards outright track duty, the 296 Speciale is a part of Ferrari's special series, meaning that customers need to have an "existing relationship" with the brand in order to get an allocation. The 296 Challenge Stradale is a standard range model, meaning anyone can walk into a dealer and order one, existing relationship or not. Ferrari claims that it wants to court newly introduced Ferrari buyers interested in experiencing the purest driving experience that the prancing horse has to offer, and the 296 CS is the first step in that direction.

U.S. pricing has not been unveiled, but in its home market, the 296 Challenge Stradale costs 291,000 euros, or the equivalent of about $320,000. Stateside deliveries of the latest CS are expected to begin sometime in late 2027. As a non-Speciale model, CS production numbers aren’t limited, which presents a unique opportunity to buy a special new Ferrari without already owning one.

Honda Recalling Thousands of S2000s for Potential Fuel Leak

💡 Key Takeaways

  • In a recent development, the reason for the recall is that the “fuel flange joint assembly may have been improperly manufactured.” As a consequence, Honda notes this could allow the fuel line connection to loosen and separate, ultimately resulting in a fuel leak and engine stall.
  • Sources indicate that honda indicates that when part production shifted locations, 67 replacement parts were produced without brazing material.

Recent findings suggest that it’s not too often we get new recalls for older cars like the Honda S2000, but today is one of those days. According to the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, Honda is recalling 16,387 S2000 roadsters from the 2004–20005 model years, the first two years of the AP2 refresh. A quick look at the sales figures for those years seems to suggest that means all (or close to all) S2000s from those years are part of the recall population.

In a recent development, the reason for the recall is that the “fuel flange joint assembly may have been improperly manufactured.” As a consequence, Honda notes this could allow the fuel line connection to loosen and separate, ultimately resulting in a fuel leak and engine stall. The problem with manufacturing relates to whether or not it was built with brazing material at the joint-to-flange connection. With the part being a push-to-fit part, Honda says this lack of material could cause the connection to become loose and separate.

Sources indicate that honda indicates that when part production shifted locations, 67 replacement parts were produced without brazing material. These parts were shipped and potentially installed in S2000s. Honda estimates the percentage of cars with the defect is 1 percent. There won’t be many warning signs before it’s too late to continue driving, but Honda says stalling, a misfire, fuel odor and an inability to start the engine are all symptoms.

As of now, Honda says there are no injuries or deaths related to this issue. Those with cars in the recall range will have to bring their convertibles into the Honda dealer for the remedy. Once there, it will receive a newly introduced and improved fuel flange joint assembly free of charge.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Developed by Japanese material handling giant Tadano, the 35-ton V320RC wheeled electric pick & carry crane has spent the last few months proving itself at NMG Italia’s job sites, where it’s been handling heavy loads in tight industrial spaces and improving efficiency by 50%. And now, you can buy one.

Developed in collaboration with NMG Italia, the V320RC electric crane has already proven its performance in the field with NMG and during precision setup operations at Marmomac, a trade show dedicated to the marble industry held each year in Verona.

“The (Tadano) V320RC marks a real breakthrough in the pick & carry industry,” reads the official Tadano launch copy. “Rather than an evolution of existing solutions, it introduces a fresh philosophy, with technologies and features capable of setting new benchmarks in the lifting market. Tadano and NMG Italia continue their collaboration in the field, turning real-world experience into new technological solutions to meet the most advanced demands of industrial lifting.”.

The crane itself is a compact, battery-electric pick-and-carry machine with a maximum lifting capacity of 35 tonnes. Measuring just 5 m long, 2.15 m wide and 2.400 m tall (a meter is about a yard, guys – you got this), the V320RC is designed to bring heavy lifting capability into tight industrial spaces where larger cranes struggle to operate.

According to recent reports, the new Tadano runs on a 120V, 1,120 Ah li-ion battery pack (that works out to ~134 kWh) and packs a gross vehicle weight of more than 31,150 kg (~34.5 short tones). That number includes 9,500 kg (~10 tons) of removable counterweights that make transport and handling easier for a wider range of customers. Under the hood, a new hydraulic system pairs a variable-displacement pump with what the tech giant calls “an electro-hydraulic control valve” to improve precision and responsiveness while reducing energy consumption.

According to NMG Italia, all that baked-in tech V320RC give them 50% better productivity than competing electric cranes working under equivalent workloads, with enough battery capacity to support several days of operation between charges.

What Teachers Know (Or Don’t Know) About Left-Handedness

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (712 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 26, 2026 | Reviewed by Kaja Perina.
  • It has been revealed that all over the world, teachers play a crucial role in their pupils' learning experience.
  • Recent findings suggest that A new study entitled “Handedness literacy in teachers: Data from Greece, Serbia, and Belgium”, just published in the scientific journal Laterality, aimed at closing this gap in the psychological literature by focusing on teachers’ handedness literacy (Papadatou-Pastou and co-workers, 2026).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 26, 2026 | Reviewed by Kaja Perina.

It has been revealed that all over the world, teachers play a crucial role in their pupils' learning experience. This is especially true for left-handed children, who, for a long time, have been forced to write with their right hand against their will in many countries. Thankfully, the awful practice of handedness relearning is now a thing of the past in the US and many other countries, and today, both left-handed and right-handed pupils are encouraged to write with their naturally dominant hand in school. This makes it notable that teachers have some basic knowledge about handedness and also the ergonomic needs of left-handed kids in learning environments. As handedness typically is not a main focus in teacher education, it is, however, largely unknown what knowledge the average teacher has about handedness and the specific learning needs of left-handed children. Thus, more psychological research on this important topic is needed.

Recent findings suggest that A new study entitled “Handedness literacy in teachers: Data from Greece, Serbia, and Belgium”, just published in the scientific journal Laterality, aimed at closing this gap in the psychological literature by focusing on teachers’ handedness literacy (Papadatou-Pastou and co-workers, 2026). Handedness literacy refers to a person’s general knowledge and understanding of handedness.

In a recent development, the study team, led by renowned handedness researcher Marietta Papadatou-Pastou, asked more than 800 prospective and in-service teachers to fill out a questionnaire with various questions about their knowledge of handedness and about themselves. The teachers came from three different European countries: Greece, Serbia, and Belgium.

The questionnaire the teachers had to fill out consisted of four main parts. The first part consisted of open-ended questions about left-handedness, such as “Do left-handed students differ from right-handed students?”. The teachers had to write answers to these questions. The second part of the questionnaire consisted of 18 questions quizzing the teachers about their knowledge of handedness. The third part of the questionnaire contained further questions about handedness, and the fourth part contained some questions about the teachers themselves, such as their own handedness and their age, among others.

The analysis of the data yielded several interesting results about teachers’ handedness literacy.

Sources indicate that the analyses of the open-ended questions about handedness in the first part of the questionnaire showed that teachers generally had a supportive attitude towards left-handed pupils. The teachers wrote about different aspects of handedness, such as the underlying neurobiology or specific challenges left-handed pupils face, or their ergonomic and classroom needs. In general, they were in favor of letting children choose which hand they like to write with.

The analysis of the handedness literacy scores revealed that teachers knew some things about handedness, but also had quite a lot of knowledge gaps. As there were 18 questions and the scientists gave 1 point per correct question, the maximum score for handedness literacy was 18. Teachers from Serbia had an average score of 8.11 (45% correct answers). Teachers from Belgium were slightly better as they had an average score of 8.85 (49% correct answers), as were teachers from Greece, who had an average score of 8.90 (49% correct answers).

So, in all three countries, teachers had less than 50% correct answers- if there were a left-handedness test, they would probably fail! One thing that many teachers got wrong was that they thought that left-handed pupils were more intelligent than right-handed pupils. Also, many teachers thought that there were more left-handers in the population than the actual percentage (10.6%). Interestingly, left-handed teachers did not show higher handedness literacy than right-handed teachers.

Recent findings suggest that many of the teachers who participated in the study stated that they thought that handedness literacy in teachers needs to be improved. The results of the study show that this is actually true. This suggests that teacher education should include more scientific information on left-handedness, so that teachers can optimally educate left-handed kids.

Industry observers note that papadatou-Pastou, M., Papadopoulou, A. K., Kovic, V., Gerrits, R., & Vingerhoets, G. (2026). Handedness literacy in teachers: Data from Greece, Serbia, and Belgium. Laterality, 1–43. Advance online publication. https://doi.org/10.1080/1357650X.2026.2753053.

#224458. Bears don’t sleep all winter, and other cold-weather animal myths

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (955 w)
📖 Baca
General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Popsci ↗ Open Full Page

Bears don’t sleep all winter, and other cold-weather animal myths

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (955 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It’s almost winter in the Northern Hemisphere.
  • According to recent reports, that brings to mind a number of misconceptions people have about animals in the winter.
  • It has been revealed that many of us learned in school or on TV that bears sleep all winter.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It’s almost winter in the Northern Hemisphere. While the humans fire up their furnaces (or, ideally, heat pumps), animals prepare in their own ways.

According to recent reports, that brings to mind a number of misconceptions people have about animals in the winter. Most of us were taught things that, over time, were proven to be untrue, and winter behaviors are no exception. Bears, for example, don’t sleep the entire winter. Birds don’t actually care about the cold that much, and migrate for other reasons. And squirrels aren’t constantly forgetting the location of their nuts. Let’s dig into these common winter myths, and what actual research points to.

It has been revealed that many of us learned in school or on TV that bears sleep all winter. It’s not true—bears don’t hibernate. At least, not exactly.

An explainer published by the National Park Service states that hibernation isn’t a black-and-white concept: “In recent years the view that the state of hibernation exists on a spectrum rather than as a binary yes-or-no condition is becoming more entrenched.” The piece goes on to say that black bears don’t hibernate as deeply as smaller animals.

There’s real research backing this up. A 2011 study published in Science by researchers at the University of Alaska Fairbanks demonstrates that bears get up and shift position throughout the winter. “Animals changed position twice a day to once every 2 days, when they stood, occasionally groomed, and rearranged bedding material,” the study states. The research also states that bears use a great deal more energy during the winter than smaller animals. “During torpor, metabolic rates of small hibernators decrease to 2 to 5 percent of basal metabolic rate (BMR),” the study explains, before showing that bears’ metabolic rates reach closer to 25 percent. That’s a wide spectrum.

It has been revealed that so bears don’t sleep all winter—they regularly get up. That brings us to another myth: The idea that bears give birth without waking up. It’s also not true, according to the National Park Service.

“They’re not only awake during this time, but in the days before birthing, expectant mothers will often add bedding to the den by chewing materials into smaller pieces and arranging them just-so,” the explainer states. “After the 1 to 3 half-ounce to 1 lb cubs are born, she meticulously licks them clean, and provides warmth and mother’s milk as they grow to about 5 lbs by the time they emerge in spring.”.

Industry observers note that which isn’t to say that bears are active in winter—they really do slow down. But they don’t hibernate to the same extent as smaller animals.

You might think that birds fly south for the winter because they don’t want to freeze—we even call cold-hating humans who travel in winter “snowbirds,” in reference to this belief. But it turns out birds aren’t directly concerned with cold weather.

If you have a bird feeder you’ve probably noticed that many birds stick around for the winter.An explainer by the Cornell Lab of Ornithology states that birds are perfectly capable of surviving winter temperatures. “Escaping cold temperatures is not itself a major factor that drives birds to migrate, since many species, even hummingbirds, can withstand freezing temperatures as long as an adequate supply of food is available,” the article states.

There’s less food around in the winter, and that’s the actual reason for migration. You might say this is semantics, and you’re not entirely wrong—the cold temperature causes the food shortage. But if you’re picturing shivering birds, desperate to travel somewhere warmer, you’re imagining the wrong motivation. Birds don’t leave in pursuit of warmer weather; they leave in pursuit of food and longer daylight hours. And they head back north (or south) in the spring for the same reason: the thaw means a lot of fresh food, not to mention safe, open areas for breeding.

Industry observers note that squirrels spend a good part of the year hiding nuts, all so they can recover them in the winter. A common legend goes something like this: squirrels forget about most of these nuts, and that’s how forests grow. And while it is true that squirrel caches can become trees, squirrels don’t forget their nuts that often.

They are, in fact, really good at keeping track of their nuts, and this has been known for decades. A 1991 paper published in Animal Behaviour by researchers at Princeton University showed this. In the study, captive grey squirrels were all given hazelnuts to bury in the same area. The nuts were then all removed by experimenters. The squirrels were re-introduced to the site, one by one, with a twist: experimenters buried fresh nuts in the squirrel’s own 10 cache sites and an equal number of sites randomly chosen from caches made by other squirrels.

The results were striking. “Although each squirrel’s own caches were close to the caches of other squirrels, the squirrels retrieved significantly more nuts from their own sites than from sites used by other squirrels, after all delays,” the paper states. “The retrieval accuracy of the squirrels under these conditions indicates that while grey squirrels can locate buried nuts by their odour, they can also remember the individual locations of nuts they have buried.”.

It has been revealed that other studies show how well squirrels can remember nuts. A 2023 study published in Urban Ecosystems by researchers from Poland found that hazelnuts cached by squirrels are more likely to be dug up than hazelnuts buried by humans in the same area. This suggests that squirrels are pretty good at remembering where they buried their nuts.

Infant Bleeding Cases Surge as More Parents Refuse Vitamin K Shots for Newborns

💡 Key Takeaways

  • A research letter, published in JAMA Pediatrics, analyzed data on approximately 11 million infants from 2017 to 2025 and found that vitamin K administration declined from 97.7% to 95%, while cases of vitamin K deficiency bleeding (VKDB) nearly quadrupled.
  • In a recent development, A second study published in JAMA, based on data from 5.2 million U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Two large studies published on November 5 link declining newborn vitamin K shot rates to a sharp increase in infant bleeding cases, including potentially fatal brain hemorrhages.

A research letter, published in JAMA Pediatrics, analyzed data on approximately 11 million infants from 2017 to 2025 and found that vitamin K administration declined from 97.7% to 95%, while cases of vitamin K deficiency bleeding (VKDB) nearly quadrupled.

In a recent development, A second study published in JAMA, based on data from 5.2 million U.S. infants, found that refusal rates more than doubled, rising from 3.1% in 2017 to 6.8% in 2025. Infants who did not receive the shot had a 47% higher risk of bleeding and more than twice the risk of intracranial bleeding.

Additionally, new data from Truveta suggest the trend is continuing: refusals of vitamin K shots increased by 57% between January and June 2026, rising from 5.2% to 8.1% of newborns.

Vitamin K is essential for blood clotting, and newborns naturally have very low levels. Without the preventive injection, infants are at risk for VKDB, which can cause sudden bleeding in the brain, gastrointestinal tract, and other organs. Late-onset VKDB can occur up to six months after birth, often without warning signs, and may be fatal.

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) continue to recommend an intramuscular vitamin K injection for all newborns, ideally within 6 hours of birth.

The shot is not a vaccine; it is a nutrient injection that helps prevent dangerous bleeding. A single dose reduces the risk of late-onset VKDB by approximately 98%.

Experts not involved in the studies attribute the rise in refusals partly to broader vaccine hesitancy and mixed public health messaging.

“The decision to vaccinate a newborn or allow a vitamin K injection at birth is complex, with multiple factors playing a role in the ultimate decision,” said Graham Tse, MD, a pediatrician and chief medical officer of MemorialCare Miller Children’s & Women’s Hospital in Long Beach, CA.

It has been revealed that some of these factors, Tse said, include conflicting messages from federal health agencies such as the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), both overseen by HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr., an outspoken critic of the childhood immunization schedule.

The vitamin K shot is not a vaccine, yet RFK Jr. has declined to reassure parents about its safety, despite the CDC’s current recommendation to administer it at birth.

Additionally, growing medical distrust among parents has led to refusal of routine newborn care, such as the vitamin K shot, Reuters reports.

Healthline spoke with Tse to learn more about the risks of refusing the vitamin K shot and what new or expectant parents should know about this routine newborn treatment.

This interview has been lightly edited and condensed for clarity and length.

Tse: The decision to vaccinate a newborn or allow a vitamin K injection at birth is complex, with multiple factors playing a role in the ultimate decision.

A contributing factor to the decline in vitamin K injection at birth, as well as in newborn hepatitis B vaccination, is the conflicting messages from the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).

Recommendations from these entities and others are conflicting or do not align with established, research-based, and proven recommendations from organizations such as the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) and the Infectious Diseases Society of America.

When there are conflicting recommendations, it creates confusion and doubt among parents about what the best or right choice is for their child.

As well, there is so much misinformation on the internet, among influencers, and on social media that it is difficult to know what information is accurate, well-researched, and proven, versus what may be just someone’s opinion or belief.

Some are mistaking the vitamin K injection at birth for a vaccination, which it is not. Ultimately, all these factors are contributing to parents declining or delaying vitamin K injections at birth.

Tse: Declining the newborn vitamin K injection puts the newborn at significant risk of serious and life threatening complications from vitamin K-deficient bleeding (VKDB). This was previously referred to as hemorrhagic disease of the newborn.

VKDB can be as mild as bruising of the skin but can be as serious as bleeding into the brain, and newborns and infants can die from VKDB.

Declining vitamin K injection at birth is significant because of the serious and potentially life threatening consequences of deficiency of Vitamin K and not being able to clot the blood.

The vitamin K injection at birth is highly effective at preventing VKDB.

Tse: If a neonate or infant has vitamin K deficiency, the ability to clot their blood and stop bleeding is highly reduced.

All newborns are at risk of low vitamin K due to low body stores, low vitamin K content of breast milk, reduced ability of the gut to mobilize vitamin K, and poor transfer of vitamin K across the placenta.

Sources indicate that when the blood cannot clot, bleeding from minor or minimal trauma can occur, and even bleeding without injury or trauma may occur. This can include bruises, bleeding from the mouth or gastrointestinal tract, bleeding from cuts or circumcision.

Bleeding can occur anywhere in the body, including in the brain, which can be catastrophic.

VKDB can occur from birth and through several months of life. Bleeding in the brain from VKDB, one of the most serious consequences, can occur at any time from birth to up to 6 months or so and can occur unexpectedly and suddenly. Vitamin K given at birth can prevent this risk of bleeding.

In a recent development, tse: Vitamin K is a necessary vitamin that all humans need. Vitamin K is not a vaccination.

Newborns need vitamin K to prevent serious, significant, and often catastrophic bleeding during their first several months of life.

Vitamin K has been given to newborns in the United States for close to 70 years, is safe, is studied, and is proven to help prevent vitamin K-deficient bleeding.

I urge newly introduced parents to allow their newborns to receive the vitamin K injection at birth — it protects them, keeps them healthy, is proven safe, and is recommended.

Sources indicate that the Illinois Clean Ports Program is putting $104 million behind efforts to help clean up its working waterfronts, funds earmarked for heavy-duty electric equipment assets that includes forklifts, giant reach stackers, switcher locomotives, and the charging equipment needed to support them. There’s even a passenger ferry!

Procurement is now underway for zero-emission vehicles, equipment, and supporting infrastructure at four sites across the state. Administered by the Illinois Environmental Protection Agency (Illinois EPA), Illinois’ Clean Ports Program aims to modernize operations at ports and waterfront facilities in Chicago, the Quad Cities, and southern Illinois’ river port districts.

“Illinois’ waterways are a competitive advantage for the state,” noted Illinois Governor JB Pritzker, who was elected to a historic third term on 03NOV. “By modernizing port infrastructure, advancing zero-emission technology, and improving air quality, we are strengthening our economy while building a cleaner future for Illinois.”.

Illinois’ Clean Ports Program isn’t just replacing diesel-powered equipment with electric alternatives – instead, the strategy also includes Level 2 and DC fast charging, shore power and charging for electrified ships, and comprehensive grid upgrades designed to modernize existing port operations and support the deployment of new electric equipment.

Recent findings suggest that the program takes a holistic approach to port electrification at Chicago’s Illinois International Port District (IIPD), treating energy generation, storage, and deployment as parts of a single connected system. On-site solar helps meet the port’s growing electricity needs while excess power is stored for peak hours, when grid electricity is most expensive. This setup reduces strain on the local grid, and acts as a hedge against rising energy costs.

Sources indicate that for smaller public port districts, replacing aging equipment and upgrading electrical infrastructure can be an enormous financial undertaking. The Illinois Clean Ports Program helps make those investments possible, bringing cleaner, healthier, zero-emission technology within reach of terminal operators while preparing the state’s ports for a more competitive freight future.

Alongside showing everything coming with this next update, the developer also declared that 3.8 will go on for eight weeks, rather than the usual six. V3.8 is dubbed "Memories are the Prelude to Dreams", and it brings an end to the Amphoreus journey.

This memory-hunting adventure is told from the perspective of Firefly, which will also explain how she entered the dreamscape initially and met the squad.

The upcoming playable character is The Dahlia, whose power is linked to the the Remembrance path, which allows her to fabricate memories. Despite taking her powers from the Remembrance, The Dhalia actually follows the Path of Nihility in-game: she’s a 5-Star character who shines in teams dealing Break DMG.

The Dhalia can unleash a Gloomy Zone that causes Toughness Reduction inflicted by allies to trigger Super Break DMG, even before you break your enemies’ Weaknesses. The Dahlia can also invite one teammate to become her Dance Partner, which allows them (and her) to deal additional Super Break DMG each time they attack an enemy. If you trigger her Ultimate after picking a Dance Partner, she applies Type Weaknesses of both partners to enemies.

Sources indicate that while The Dahlia is the only new character appearing in this final Amphoreus upgrade, there'll be reruns aplenty, with an unusual third banner phase to make up for the extra long wait for 4.0. Appropriately for her role in the story, Firefly will make her return alongside The Dahlia in Phase 1, while Fugue and Lingsha will both have banner reruns in Phase 2, which is expected on January 7th. A bonus two-week-long Phase 3 will then begin on January 28th, seeing brief reappearances for popular returning characters Aglaea and Sunday, before things (presumably) go back to normal with the new annual update.

According to recent reports, something else to look forward to in 3.8 is The Chrysos Awoo Championship, which invites players to become chimera trainers and compete in team-based battles. The Remnants of Twilight event kicks off with the newly introduced patch, too, featuring its own set of challenges. However, HoYoverse have confirmed that there won't be an extra event during Phase 3 — but hopefully that'll give you some time to wrap up the last of the Amphoreus story content, which is longer than the previous four chapters put together.

Mysterious volcanic rock discovered in the Mariana Trench

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (821 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Space exploration tends to suck up most of the oxygen when it comes to venturing out into the unknown.
  • That absurd depth and bone-crushing pressure make Challenger Deep brutally difficult to study.
  • In a recent development, using the remotely operated Jason/Medea submarine robot, the team documented evidence of pyroclastic rocks (the shattered debris of violent eruptions) on the trench wall some 20,000 feet below the surface.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Space exploration tends to suck up most of the oxygen when it comes to venturing out into the unknown. But there’s an arguably even more mysterious frontier hidden beneath us. Nowhere is that more real than at Challenger Deep. The deepest known point on Earth, Challenger Deep is located in the 1,580-mile-long Mariana Trench at the floor of the Pacific Ocean. Getting to the bottom of this ancient chasm means diving more than 6.8 miles (around 36,000 feet) underwater. For a sense of scale, Mount Everest could be dropped into this chasm, and its summit still wouldn’t reach the surface.

That absurd depth and bone-crushing pressure make Challenger Deep brutally difficult to study. As a result, assumptions about what lies down there rarely hold up for long. Scientists long believed the area’s frigid, pitch-dark depths couldn’t sustain life, until a pair of divers reported animals near the seafloor in 1960. Now, a team using a robotic submersible in the trench claims they have found the deepest evidence of explosive volcanic eruptions ever documented in the ocean.

In a recent development, using the remotely operated Jason/Medea submarine robot, the team documented evidence of pyroclastic rocks (the shattered debris of violent eruptions) on the trench wall some 20,000 feet below the surface. Finding those kinds of rocks there was unexpected and will change the way geologists view the area. Writing today in the journal Frontiers in Earth Science, the researchers say their discoveries may also “help explain why the Challenger Deep is so deep.”.

It has been revealed that “Explosive volcanism near trenches is unusual, so we were very surprised,” Dr. Robert J. Stern, a geologist at the University of Texas at Dallas and study co-author, noted in a statement. “These are the deepest pyroclastic rocks documented to date from anywhere in the ocean.”.

Reaching the depth needed to study the Mariana Trench takes some serious equipment and preparation. In 2012, Titanic director James Cameron famously made the dive with a specially designed submersible that reportedly cost around $10 million to build. In this case, the team of scientists turned to a veteran robotic system called Jason/Medea. Part of the National Deep Submergence Facility and funded by the National Science Foundation, Jason/Medea traces its earliest version back to 1988. From the outside, the ROV somewhat resembles a Zamboni machine used to surface ice skating rinks.

The robot can operate as deep as 21,385 feet below the surface, thanks to a roughly six-mile long fiber-optic cable connecting it to a vessel on the surface. Jason is equipped with a video and still-imaging systems. Its footage travels up through Medea, a companion robot that  hangs slightly higher in the water to buffer Jason from the motion of the vessel above. In addition to taking photos and videos, Jason has mechanical arms he can use to collect rock and sediment samples. The robotic duo has completed hundreds of dives around the world, analyzing hydrothermal vents in the Atlantic and Pacific Ocean, and even visiting a 1,600-year-old sunken Roman trading ship.

Recent findings suggest that in this case, the scientists deployed their robot companion in late 2024 along a 341 mile segment of the trench near Challenger Deep. Over seven dives, the robot team covered around 186 miles, taking photos and videos along the way. Analyzing the footage, the human team determined that the eastern part of the stretch is deeper than the western part and has steeper trench walls. They came across the old volcanic rocks on that steeper western side, seen below arranged in a thin flat layer. Exactly where these rocks erupted from remains unclear.

In a recent development, ”We haven’t identified the eruption sites yet,” Stern added. “We know that these hot pyroclastic flows moved down slopes, but we don’t think they moved very far. They retained enough heat to re-weld themselves into pretty hard rocks, and that heat would’ve been lost if the pyroclastic flows traveled great distances.”.

Sources indicate that the unexpected rocks were only one part of the expedition. The team also set out to study fragments of older, exposed crust and mantle. They also tasked the robot with studying the Shinaki Seep Field, one of deepest known hydrothermal vents sites on the planet. There was some cleanup duty as well:  the team recovered fluid-sampling devices left behind by a previous group of Japanese scientists in 2016. Explorers have rather glibly documented human trash all the way down at the bottom of Challenger Deep but these scientists, at least, won’t be adding to the litter.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • When people spend nearly $2 million on a two-seat, mid-engine car, you can safely assume it is not the only car in their garage.
  • But Spyker CEO Victor Muller has a different idea.
  • That's a refreshing philosophy from someone selling a car this pricey.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When people spend nearly $2 million on a two-seat, mid-engine car, you can safely assume it is not the only car in their garage. It makes sense that it will not be driven every day; however, often times cars like this are not really driven at all. They spend their entire lives in climate-controlled garages, tucked beneath soft covers. And when the car in question is something like a one-of-25 C8 Preliator XXV Coupé, the temptation to preserve it as a collectible is understandable.

But Spyker CEO Victor Muller has a different idea. He wants his customers to get behind the wheel and drive. "We prefer to sell our cars to people that actually use them," Muller told me during an interview at Retromobile Upcoming York. "Because that's what I made them for. To drive the hell out of them.".

That's a refreshing philosophy from someone selling a car this pricey. Particularly when that car is the new C8 Preliator XXV Coupé, which looks as much like a piece of fine jewelry as an 800-horsepower road rocket. Unfortunately, Muller admits that many of Spyker's previous creations haven't enjoyed particularly active lives.

"Many of our cars, of the 252 we made so far, have just ended up in dungeons, in vaults, in spaces where nobody will ever see them," Muller said. He's hoping to change that by organizing more owner events and encouraging customers to spend time enjoying their cars; Spyker has joined the Supercar Owners Circle, a global network of car collectors, and is planning gatherings in Europe and the United States.

Industry observers note that the firm is also in a position where it can be selective about who gets its cars. According to Muller, all 25 Preliator XXV Coupés sold during their debut at The Quail, a Motorsports Gathering in August. Every single one was snapped up in a day. "I've never seen anything like that in my entire life," he said. Spyker intends to build 25 Spyders and 25 Sedancas in 2028, he added, once production of the Coupés is complete next year.

Industry observers note that who is buying these cars has changed dramatically over the last quarter century. "In 2000, my typical customer was a fifty-five to sixty-year-old industrialist—old money, car collector, very astute buyer," Muller explained. "Fast forward twenty five years. Your average age is thirty-five years. Tech investor. Huge collection. Knows his cars completely. But nobody asks how much it is.".

Sources indicate that muller says approximately 40 percent of his new buyers are existing or former Spyker owners, and roughly 80 percent of the new cars are expected to go to the United States. But no matter how old the buyer is or where they live, Muller wants them to drive the cars. This makes sense when you understand his approach to engineering; The new car has no massive infotainment screens or hybrid systems, and electronic intervention is largely limited to essential safety features like ABS and stability control.

Sources indicate that “If you mis-shift in a Spyker and you drive two hundred miles an hour and you shift to second gear, you blow up the engine," Muller mentioned. "And I think it has to be that way in Spyker world." For Spyker, the connection between driver and machine is more important than chasing lap records, acceleration figures and electronic nannies. "If you don't like that, buy something else," he added. "If not, man up—drive a Spyker.".

According to recent reports, another way to demonstrate that these cars are meant to be driven is to get the brand back into racing. Muller revealed that Spyker is taking steps toward returning to professional endurance competition. The tech giant competed in the 24 Hours of Le Mans eight times, most recently in 2010. Naturally, I asked whether another trip to Le Mans might be in Spyker's future.

"Absolutely," Muller noted. "We'd love to go back in racing." Muller says Spyker is preparing to re-enter endurance racing, although he stopped short of announcing a timeline, championship, or confirmed race entry. He certainly likes the idea of seeing his latest creation on the track. More importantly, he's already started putting people in place to make it happen.

"I actually hired my former GT2 race director again," Muller said. "He started a week ago today.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For decades, Briggs & Stratton has helped keep the lights on after the storm with its gas-powered generators. Now, the manufacturer is bringing that legacy to the electric age with a new 16 kWh backup battery designed to scale with your growing energy needs.

According to recent reports, briggs & Stratton partnered with Texas-based EG4 to offer an all American-branded solution for battery backup power solution last year, and its stackable SimpliPHI batteries helped make it easy to right-size home battery projects – but those batteries were limited in size, and limited in what they could actually offer. With the launch of the brand’s new, 16 kWh SimpliPHI battery, the organization is ready to meet your energy needs … even if those needs take you up to 512 kWh. (!).

For context, the average US home uses about 865 kWh of energy per month, so a 512 kWh battery should theoretically keep your lights on for nearly 18 days after a storm – or provide basic power for your whole block for a weekend, at least!

In a recent development, “This launch represents a significant shift in our battery strategy,” explains Sequoya Cross, vice president of energy storage at Briggs & Stratton. “Our combined resources allow us to bring a competitively priced battery of the highest quality to energy storage installers.”.

An onboard battery management system (BMS) and built-in Wi-Fi gateway help to streamline the system’s setup for installers, while the Briggs battery’s automatic inverter sensing technology supports closed-loop communication with Sol-Ark, Solis, EG4, Growatt, Megarevo, Victron, and other leading inverters. Other installer-friendly features include an IP65-rated enclosure allows for indoor or outdoor installation in either ground- or wall-mounted setups without requiring an additional cabinet, and an integrated circuit breaker that allows technicians to isolate the battery during servicing.

The battery itself is rated for 8,000 cycles at 90% depth of discharge, with a charge and discharge rate of 0.5C and an end-of-life capacity of 70%. Briggs & Stratton backs its upcoming battery packs with a 12-year parts warranty that includes labor and travel costs, as well as a US-based tech support service.

The SimpliPHI 16 is available for pre-order now, though pricing was not mentioned in the original press release.

SOURCE: Briggs & Stratton Energy Solutions.
